channel.title: Synthetic Musings
channel.description: Technical write-ups on machine learning, statistics, linear algebra, and the tooling around them, by Ravi Kalia.

item.title: The Two Cultures, Part 5: The Pushback, and What Prediction Cannot Tell You
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
Breiman’s paper was published with four comments and a reply, and the comment he answered with “I agree.” raises the question predictive accuracy cannot settle: what happens if we change something.

Every predictive model invites the same misreading. A churn model ranks discount codes among its top features, a readmission model gives a drug a large importance score, and the next meeting asks what happens if the company sends more codes or the hospital prescribes more of the drug. The model was never asked that question. It learned which customers and which patients tend to have which outcomes, and the people who get discounts or drugs are not a random sample. Cox’s comment makes this point in 2001, and it is the point Breiman conceded.

Parts 1–4 re-ran the paper’s evidence. This part sets the discussants against those results and then takes up Cox’s question with a widget and with data whose causal answer is known from an experiment.

This part covers two ideas:

  • The pushback. Four statisticians answered Breiman in print; each comment, in its strongest form, survives some of the re-runs and is contradicted by others.
  • Prediction against intervention. A model can predict an outcome well and still answer an intervention question wrongly, because the data record who was treated, not what treatment does.

1 The discussion

Statistical Science printed the paper with four invited comments and Breiman’s reply (pp. 216–231). Breiman sorted them himself in the rejoinder’s first paragraph (p. 226).

Each subsection states the comment in its strongest form, then what the re-runs in Parts 1–4 do to it.

1.1 Cox: start from the question, and know what you are predicting

Cox grants more than his reputation for the opposing view suggests. He calls work without an explicit probability model a legitimate part of statistics, and he accepts that a purely empirical predictor sometimes wins; short-term economic forecasting and real-time flood forecasting are his examples (p. 216). His objections are four.

  1. The picture of mainstream practice is a caricature. His word; he adds that good caricatures expose real weaknesses (p. 216). Journal papers illustrate technique, while live analyses that reach conclusions are reported in subject-matter journals and reports, so the journals Breiman read are the wrong sample (p. 217).
  2. Data have a meaning before they have a model. What a variable measures, how the cases were ascertained, measurement error and why values are missing all bear on the answer, and he doubts these can be handled without some probabilistic model (p. 216).
  3. Much prediction worth doing is extrapolation. His examples: the course of the vCJD epidemic in the UK, and the effect on US cancer incidence of cutting medical X-ray use by 10% (p. 216). Both ask what happens under conditions the data never showed, and the second asks what an intervention would do. A predictor validated on a random test set from the same population says nothing about either.
  4. A model should carry subject-matter meaning. He lists Cox and Wermuth’s requirements: connect to background knowledge, point toward a generating process, have parameters with a clear interpretation, specify the noise well enough to state precision, and fit adequately. Fit, which predictive accuracy measures, is last and is not the basis of choice (p. 217). The aim is descriptions that are potentially causal (p. 218).

Two smaller points land on specific results. Cox warns that complete separation, on which Breiman’s SVM argument rests, is unstable, and that the bootstrap and cross-validation may give “a quite misleading illusion of stability” (p. 218). He also quotes an aphorism he attributes, tentatively, to Kelvin: a rough answer to the right question beats an exact answer to the wrong one (p. 218).

What the re-runs say:

  • Point 2 holds. The Bupa “class” in Part 4 is a train/test selector created by the people who collected the data; a forest predicted it with 25% error and no amount of accuracy could reveal what it was. The hepatitis file’s binary codes are documented only by the data themselves.
  • The separation warning holds. In Part 4’s forward-selection bootstrap, sex is chosen in 81% of resamples because no woman in the data died.
  • Point 3 is the one Breiman conceded, and the subject of Section 2.

1.2 Efron: where did the bias go?

Efron reads the paper as a call for theory, not against it.

  1. Twentieth-century statistics was “100 years of unbiasedness” (p. 218). Unbiased estimation needs a favourable ratio of sample size to parameters, and good design exists to secure it.
  2. Black boxes with many knobs must be biased estimators. Regularisation, tree pruning and SVM margins all trade variance for bias somewhere, and there is little theory for heavily biased estimators (p. 219).
  3. Two rules of thumb about comparisons (p. 219). New methods always look better than old ones, because honest simulation comparisons are hard and the old method rarely gets the same tuning effort. Complicated methods are harder to criticise than simple ones.
  4. Prediction is rarely enough. The post office needs only addresses read correctly; Gregory studied the hepatitis data partly to understand the disease, and most surveys aim at causal factors (p. 219).
  5. The hepatitis variables. From his fuller analysis with Gong (1983): variables 12 or 17 were selected in 60% of bootstrap samples, against 59% for variable 19 (p. 219). He asks in what sense a variable is important.

What the re-runs say:

  • Rule 1. Every single tree in Part 3 was pruned by cross-validation inside its training data, and the forest was not tuned. The forest still won on all ten sets.
  • Point 2 has an answer for one model family. In Part 3’s double-descent curve the bias hides in which interpolating fit least squares picks: the one of smallest norm.
  • Point 5. Part 4 found importance depends on the model, the measure and the correlation among inputs; Breiman’s rejoinder says the same.

1.3 Hoadley: an algorithmic culture inside the data-modeling toolbox

Hoadley wrote from Fair, Isaac, where credit scoring had been algorithmic since the 1960s (p. 220). He agrees with Breiman’s direction and disputes the details.

  1. “Primitive” is wrong. Fair, Isaac’s segmented scorecards were built by engineers: thousands of derived characteristics, a shallow tree of segments, and a binned additive score in each leaf, about 10,000 features from 24 raw inputs, judged only on test samples (pp. 220–221).
  2. Accuracy and interpretability can coexist. The Fat Scorecard, logistic regression on binned dummies, slightly beat a 2,000-weight neural network and held up on three later test samples (p. 222).
  3. The test sample is not the future. It samples the current population; scorecards are rebuilt every 18–24 months (pp. 221–222). Tuning that peeks at the test sample biases the estimate (p. 223).
  4. Error rate is not the objective. A fraud model is judged by dollars saved at a fixed review rate (p. 223).
  5. Importance is not a property of the variable. If an equally accurate model exists without , then is unimportant to that model (p. 223).

What the re-runs say:

  • Point 2 reproduces. On Taiwan credit-card data in Part 3, a 78-coefficient scorecard matched a 500-tree forest in AUC on three splits.
  • Point 5 reproduces. The 175 ozone regressions within 5% of the best in Part 2 use every one of the 30 candidate variables between them.

1.4 Parzen: management and science

  1. Two goals, renamed. Prediction is “management” (short-run, profit, decisions); information is “science” (long-run truth and understanding) (p. 224).
  2. Wrong model, right arithmetic. Fitting a model that misdescribes nature is the right answer to the wrong question, the error of the third kind (p. 224).
  3. Two checks to make routine. Test whether inputs are dependent, since correlated inputs act as proxies and make equally good models disagree; and test for conditional clustering, where one class occupies two separate regions of input space (pp. 224–225).
  4. Many cultures, not two. He offers his quantile-based approach and “statistical methods mining” as a synthesis (p. 225).

What the re-runs say: point 3 names both of Part 4’s findings in advance. The first check is the ascites–albumin surrogate pair; the second is Breiman’s Bupa clusters.

1.5 Breiman’s rejoinder

  1. To Cox. Data models are useful when the mechanism is well understood, or when data are too few and a policy decision is due anyway. On extrapolation and intervention he quotes Cox’s v-CJD passage and replies “I agree.” (p. 227). On the caricature he says the dispute is over the word “mainstream”: counted by SAS licences and canned-package users, his version wins by at least 100 to 1 (p. 228).
  2. To Efron. Science moves from simple models to complex ones; the job is to extract information from the most accurate model available (p. 229). A model barely better than the baseline cannot be trusted to identify causal factors (p. 229). Random forests have one tuning parameter (p. 230).
  3. On importance. Importance has always been defined operationally, and his definition is predictive. It lacks a theoretical definition and depends on the dependence among inputs: “The problem begs for research.” (p. 230).
  4. To Hoadley. Models must be rebuilt with data from the new context, and Fair, Isaac is an exception on interpretability (pp. 230–231).
  5. To Parzen. Two cultures, because the line is clear: is the analyst modeling the inside of the box or not (p. 231).

2 Prediction and intervention

2.1 Three tasks

Hernán, Hsu and Healy (2019) sort data-science work into three tasks:

  1. Description: summarise the data (what fraction of patients were readmitted).
  2. Prediction: map inputs to outputs (which patients will be readmitted).
  3. Counterfactual prediction: what the outcome would be under a different action (how many would be readmitted if all got the drug).

Breiman’s validation, held-out predictive accuracy, checks task 2. Cox’s X-ray question is task 3. Pearl’s “ladder of causation” (Pearl and Mackenzie 2018) draws the same line between seeing and doing; an earlier post works through it, and another separates attributing a model’s output from explaining the world.

The two tasks agree only when the people who received the action are comparable to those who did not. When something drives both who gets the action and the outcome, a confounder, the association in the data mixes the action’s effect with the confounder’s.

2.2 A confounder, in miniature

The widget is synthetic. It stands in for a clinical setting in which sicker patients get more of a treatment.

  • Severity .
  • Dose : sicker patients get more.
  • Outcome : severity hurts the outcome () and the dose helps ().

A model that predicts from learns the slope . Raising everyone’s dose by one unit changes by , whatever and are.

  1. At the starting setting (, , ) the fit of outcome on dose has a slope of −0.96 and an of 0.51: a respectable predictive model that says more dose means a worse outcome. The causal effect is +0.50. Adjusting for severity gives a slope of 0.49.
  2. Drag “Severity → dose” to 0. The two lines nearly coincide: with no confounding the predictive slope estimates the causal one, and the drops, because dose no longer carries information about severity.
  3. Press New patients a few times at the starting setting. The predictive slope stays between −1.0 and −0.8 over the first five draws: the error is not noise, and more data will not remove it.

The predictive model is not wrong. It answers the question it was trained on: among patients like these, who will do badly. The doctor’s question is different.

2.3 Lalonde: a predictive model against an experiment

2.3.1 Data

  • Source. The National Supported Work (NSW) demonstration, a 1970s US job-training program that assigned applicants to training or control at random. LaLonde (1986) compared the experimental estimate of its effect on earnings with non-experimental estimates built from survey comparison groups. The version here is Dehejia and Wahba’s (1999): 185 trained men and 260 controls from the experiment, and 2,490 men from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) as a comparison group. Files from Dehejia’s data page; provenance in the series’ data/README.md.
  • Variables. 1978 earnings (the outcome), training, age, education, race, marital status, whether a high-school degree, and 1974 and 1975 earnings.
  • Why this data. The experiment gives the causal answer, so every observational method can be graded against it.
  • Cost of a wrong answer. A policy funded or cut on the wrong sign.

The observational question replaces the experiment’s controls with the PSID men, who are older, better paid and more likely to be married than the program’s applicants.

Code 
L = cache.obj("lalonde_v1", causal.lalonde)


def usd(v):
    """Dollars for Markdown: escaped sign (so MathJax leaves it alone), true minus."""
    return ("−" if v < 0 else "") + f"\\${abs(v):,.0f}"


def rng(key):
    v = L[key]
    return f"{usd(min(v))} to {usd(max(v))}"


rows = [
    ("Experiment: treated minus experimental controls", f"{usd(L['experimental'])} (SE {usd(L['experimental_se'])})", "the benchmark"),
    ("Difference in means, treated vs PSID", usd(L["naive"]), "the raw association"),
    ("Linear regression on training and covariates", usd(L["ols"]), "adjusts linearly"),
    ("Random forest, read as partial dependence", rng("s_learner"), "five seeds"),
    ("Double ML, partially linear model", rng("dml_plr"), f"five seeds; SE about {usd(np.mean(L['dml_plr_se']))}"),
    ("Doubly robust effect on the treated", rng("aipw_att"), f"five seeds; SE about {usd(np.mean(L['aipw_att_se']))}"),
]
md(pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Estimate", "Effect of training on 1978 earnings", "Notes"]))
Code 
est = [("Difference in means", [L["naive"]]), ("Linear regression", [L["ols"]]),
       ("Forest, partial dependence", L["s_learner"]), ("Double ML, partially linear", L["dml_plr"]),
       ("Doubly robust, effect on treated", L["aipw_att"])]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.5, 2.6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 3]}, sharey=True)
for ax in axes:
    ax.axvspan(L["experimental"] - 2 * L["experimental_se"], L["experimental"] + 2 * L["experimental_se"],
               color=RULE, alpha=0.6, lw=0)
    ax.axvline(L["experimental"], color=INK, ls="--", lw=1)
    for k, (name, vals) in enumerate(est):
        ax.scatter(vals, [len(est) - 1 - k] * len(vals), color=[AMBER, BLUE, PURPLE, PINK, TEAL][k], s=22, zorder=3)
axes[0].set_xlim(-16500, -13500)
axes[0].set_xticks([-15000], ["−15,000"])
axes[1].set_xlim(-2500, 4000)
axes[1].set_xticks([-2000, 0, 2000, 4000], ["−2,000", "0", "2,000", "4,000"])
axes[0].set_yticks(range(len(est))[::-1], [n for n, _ in est])
axes[0].spines["right"].set_visible(False)
axes[1].spines["left"].set_visible(False)
axes[1].tick_params(left=False)
fig.supxlabel("effect on 1978 earnings (dollars); left panel: the raw difference, on its own scale", fontsize=8.5)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
  • The association is not the effect. Trained men earned \\\\$15,205 less in 1978 than the PSID men. The program selected men with low earnings; that is the confounding.
  • The forest predicts earnings moderately well: cross-validated of 0.31.
  • Its partial dependence lands near the experiment. Setting training to 1 and to 0 for every trained man and averaging the difference gives \\\\$1,340 to \\\\$1,416. Because the forest sees the earnings history and demographics that drove selection, its comparison is between similar men.
  • The doubly robust estimate of the effect on the treated, \\\\$1,317 to \\\\$2,006 with a standard error near \\\\$778, is consistent with the experiment.
  • The partially linear double-ML estimate is negative, −\\\\$1,216 to −\\\\$921. It estimates a different quantity: an average of individual effects weighted by how uncertain each man’s treatment status is given his covariates, which here means the minority of PSID men who resemble the trainees. 69% of the PSID men have a fitted probability of training below 1%, so the two targets weight very different men, and with effects that vary between men they need not agree.

The lesson differs from the widget’s. Here the confounders were measured, and a flexible predictive model with all of them recovered roughly the right answer. But the estimates span a range of thousands of dollars, including both signs, depending on the target and the method. Without the experiment there would be no way to tell from the data which one to believe. Dehejia and Wahba (1999) made the same point with propensity scores: the estimates depend on whether the comparison group overlaps with the treated.

2.4 A proxy outcome

Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli and Mullainathan (2019) studied a commercial algorithm used to refer US patients to care-management programs. It predicted future health-care costs well, and costs were used as a stand-in for health needs. Because less money was spent on Black patients than on white patients with the same needs, Black patients assigned the same risk score were sicker. The prediction was accurate; the question it answered, who will cost the most, was not the question the referral program asked, who needs help most. It is Parzen’s error of the third kind and Cox’s point about the meaning of the data, at national scale.

3 Since 2001

The paper is still argued over. A few later lines, briefly:

  • To explain or to predict (Shmueli 2010): explanatory and predictive modeling differ in goals, data, methods and validation, and conflating them misleads in both directions.
  • Prediction, estimation and attribution (Efron 2020): prediction algorithms succeed by not committing to a model, which is why their output is hard to attribute to individual inputs; the scientific uses of statistics need the other two.
  • The Rashomon set (Semenova, Rudin and Parr 2022; Fisher, Rudin and Dominici 2019): see Part 2.
  • Underspecification (D’Amour et al. 2022): equally accurate models diverge under distribution shift, Hoadley’s “the test sample is not the future” in deep learning.
  • Calibrated and conformal uncertainty. Modern neural networks can be accurate and badly calibrated (Guo et al. 2017). Conformal prediction wraps any black box in prediction sets with guaranteed coverage under exchangeability (Angelopoulos and Bates 2023), one answer to Cox’s demand for a statement of precision.
  • Twenty years on. Observational Studies 7(1) (2021) reprinted the paper with new commentary from more than two dozen authors or teams (introduction by Mitra). Many titles alone show the drift: “A Melting Pot” (Tibshirani and Hastie), “From Two Cultures to One” (Neufeld and Witten), “You Don’t Have to Choose Sides” (Miller, Foti and Fox), “Revisiting Rashomon” (D’Amour), and causal readings from Pearl and from Ogburn and Shpitser.

4 An analogy from the schools

This section is an analogy, not history: neither Ockham nor Aquinas had anything to say about regression.

  • Two views of universals. Ockham was a nominalist: only individual things exist, and general terms are names or concepts that sort them. Aquinas held a moderate realism: the common natures of things are real, existing in the individuals, and the intellect abstracts them. The data-modeling culture resembles the realist, treating a parameter as a feature of nature to be estimated. The algorithmic culture resembles the nominalist, treating a model as a useful way of sorting cases with no claim about what is inside the box. Breiman named his second lesson after Ockham for the razor; the nominalism fits him better.
  • Two kinds of knowing. Aquinas distinguishes demonstration propter quid, which reasons from a cause to its effect, from demonstration quia, which reasons from an effect, better known to us, back to the fact of its cause (Summa Theologiae I, q. 2, a. 2, following Aristotle’s distinction between knowing that and knowing why in Posterior Analytics I.13). A predictive model gives knowledge quia, that the outcome follows these inputs. The intervention question asks for knowledge propter quid, what the dose does. The analogy’s point is the old one: the first kind does not license the second.

5 What held up

  • Breiman was right that held-out accuracy should be reported. It is now routine, and his Table 2 reproduces closely on the same data 25 years later (Part 3).
  • He was right that equally good models tell different stories (Part 2), and that selecting one of them and reading its coefficients is unsafe.
  • He was partly right that an accurate black box gives better information. The forest predicted hepatitis deaths a little better than logistic regression (14.9% against 16.0% error), and best-subset logistic regression picked 205 different variable sets in 500 resamples (Part 2). But the forest’s own ranking was not steady either: over 30 bootstrap resamples albumin’s rank among the 19 covariates ran from 1 to 16 and ascites’ from 1 to 17. Importance under correlation is fragile, as he admitted (Part 4).
  • The critics were right that a goodness-of-fit test is not always blind. In Part 1 a directed test detected a nonlinearity well before a forest could use it; it failed when the nonlinearity lay where the test did not look.
  • Hoadley was right that accuracy does not force opacity, at least on credit data (Part 3).
  • Cox was right about the question. Accuracy on a random test set validates task 2. Policy, medicine and science usually ask task 3, and Breiman agreed.

6 Reproduction status

Code

     f"forest RMSE {S1['rf_rmse_lo']:.2f}–{S1['rf_rmse_hi']:.2f} vs selected regression {S1['quad_rmse']:.2f}; false alarms for all", "stand-in"),

Every part has its own table with the details; the code for every number is in its folded cells and in posts/two-cultures-breiman-2001/src/.

7 Session

pkgs = ["numpy", "pandas", "scipy", "scikit-learn", "statsmodels", "matplotlib"]
print(f"Python {platform.python_version()} on {platform.system()} {platform.machine()}")

Python 3.12.13 on Darwin arm64

The full pinned environment for the series is each post’s requirements.txt.

Forests. Predict. Experiments. Decide. Cox. Asked. The. Question. Breiman. Agreed.

item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
A random forest cannot be read the way a regression can, and Breiman’s section 11 argues that it can still say more reliably which inputs matter.

The usual objection to a black box is the one Breiman quotes from his biostatistician friends: doctors can interpret logistic regression (p. 209). His reply turns the objection round. A model’s coefficients are information only if the model fits nature, and a logistic regression that barely beats guessing is reporting on itself. A more accurate model, even an opaque one, is closer to nature’s box, so the variables it relies on are better evidence. He puts it in one line: “The goal is not interpretability, but accurate information.” (p. 210).

Part 2 found that the hepatitis variables ascites and albumin swap places in trees and in selected logistic models. This part re-runs the three analyses of Breiman’s section 11 and then tests the tool he uses for all of them, permutation importance. Part 5 asks what “important” can mean for a decision.

This part covers two ideas:

  • Importance from accuracy. Permute one input among cases the model did not train on and measure how much worse it predicts. The measure needs no coefficients, so it works for any model.
  • Its fragility. When inputs are correlated, permuting one of them creates cases that do not exist, and the measure splits credit between surrogates in ways that depend on the model and the sample.

1 Data

All three data sets are the ones Breiman used, or as close as can be found.

  • Hepatitis. 155 patients, 19 covariates, survival or death. Donated to the UCI repository by Gail Gong, from Peter Gregory’s study at Stanford Medical School; earlier analyses by Gong (1982 thesis), Diaconis and Efron (1983) and Cestnik, Kononenko and Bratko (1987). The clinical aim was to know which findings predict death, so a wrong variable list misleads the next physician who uses it. 75 patients have at least one missing value (prothrombin time is missing for 67); every model here fills them with training-set medians, since the paper does not say how they were handled.
  • Bupa liver disorders. 345 men, five blood tests and a count of daily drinks, from BUPA Medical Research, via UCI. Breiman treats the seventh column as the class, severity of liver malfunction. Section 4 shows it is not.
  • Lymphoma. Breiman’s own file: 81 samples, 4,682 genes, three classes, taken from an archived copy of his random-forests web page, where his example program reads it. The samples are from Alizadeh et al. (2000) as prepared by Dudoit, Fridlyand and Speed (2002). The file carries no gene names and no class names; class counts of 29, 43 and 9 match Dudoit et al.’s B-CLL, DLBCL and FL, which is how the labels are inferred.

Sources, access dates, licences and checksums are in the series’ data/README.md.

2 Hepatitis

2.1 Which variable is which

Breiman refers to covariates by number. The UCI documentation counts the class as attribute 1, so its numbers are one higher. Efron’s comment settles which convention Breiman used: Breiman’s variables 12 or 17 are “13 or 18 in Efron and Gong’s numbering” (p. 219). Breiman counts covariates only.

Code 
miss = np.isnan(X).sum(0)
roles = {6: "Gregory", 7: "LR top |z| (Breiman)", 11: "LR top |z| (Breiman)", 12: "RF top (Breiman)",
         14: "Gregory", 17: "RF top (Breiman)", 19: "Gregory"}
mapping = pd.DataFrame({"Breiman": range(1, 20), "UCI .names": range(2, 21), "Covariate": names,
                        "Missing": miss,
                        "Named in the paper as": [roles.get(k, "") for k in range(1, 20)]})
md(mapping)

Two checks support the mapping beyond Efron’s sentence. Breiman says 12 and 17 are highly correlated (p. 212): in these data ascites and albumin are each other’s strongest correlate. And his single-variable logistic errors, 15.7% for 12 and 19.3% for 17 (p. 212), are close to the 16.1% and 19.7% re-computed in Table 2. Gregory’s variables 6, 12, 14 and 19 (p. 210) are malaise, ascites, bilirubin and histology.

The documentation lists each clinical finding’s values as “no, yes” but does not give their numeric codes. The data do. Of the 20 patients coded 1 for ascites, 70% died, against 13% of the 130 coded 2, and their mean albumin is 3.0 against 4.0. Fluid in the abdomen and low blood albumin go together in failing livers, so code 1 means present.

2.2 Errors

The protocol is Breiman’s: 100 repetitions, each holding out a random 10% of patients, the same splits for every model.

Code 
z = B.standardized_coefficients(X, y)
top2 = list(np.argsort(-np.abs(z))[:2])


def cols(js):
    return lambda Xm: Xm[:, js]


def run_errors():
    specs = {
        "lr_all": (list(range(19)), "lr"), "rf_all": (list(range(19)), "rf"),
        "lr_top2": (top2, "lr"), "lr_12": ([ASC], "lr"), "lr_17": ([ALB], "lr"),
        "rf_12": ([ASC], "rf"), "rf_17": ([ALB], "rf"), "rf_12_17": ([ASC, ALB], "rf"),
        "lr_no12": ([j for j in range(19) if j != ASC], "lr"),
        "lr_no17": ([j for j in range(19) if j != ALB], "lr"),
    }
    out = {}
    for k, (js, kind) in specs.items():
        make = (lambda r: B.logit()) if kind == "lr" else (lambda r: B.rf(r))
        out[k] = B.holdout({k: make}, X[:, js], y)[k].to_numpy()
    return pd.DataFrame(out)


hep = cache.frame("hep_errors_v1", run_errors)
e = hep.mean()
base = float(y.mean())
rows = [
    ("Call every patient a survivor", "—", "20.6", f"{base:.1%}"),
    ("Logistic regression, all 19", "—", "17.4", f"{e['lr_all']:.1%}"),
    ("Random forest, all 19", "—", "12.3", f"{e['rf_all']:.1%}"),
    ("Logistic, top two by |coef/se|", f"{top2[0] + 1}, {top2[1] + 1}", "22.9 (on 7, 11)", f"{e['lr_top2']:.1%}"),
    ("Logistic, ascites only", "12", "15.7", f"{e['lr_12']:.1%}"),
    ("Logistic, albumin only", "17", "19.3", f"{e['lr_17']:.1%}"),
    ("Forest, ascites only", "12", "14.3", f"{e['rf_12']:.1%}"),
    ("Forest, albumin only", "17", "14.3", f"{e['rf_17']:.1%}"),
    ("Forest, ascites and albumin", "12, 17", "no better than one", f"{e['rf_12_17']:.1%}"),
    ("Logistic, all but ascites", "—", "little change", f"{e['lr_no12']:.1%}"),
    ("Logistic, all but albumin", "—", "little change", f"{e['lr_no17']:.1%}"),
]
tab = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Model", "Variables", "Breiman (%)", "Here"])
md(tab)
  • The forest beats logistic regression, 14.9% against 16.0%, but by less than Breiman’s 12.3% against 17.4%. His forest’s 30% reduction is 7% here.
  • The top two coefficients are not the top two variables. The two largest standardised coefficients here are spiders (np.int64(11)) and bilirubin (np.int64(14)); Breiman’s were 7 and 11. A logistic model on those two alone does worse than the full model, 17.6%, as his did.
  • Either surrogate alone does most of the work. Ascites alone in a logistic model gives 16.1%, level with all 19 variables together.

2.3 Which variables matter

Breiman’s two figures put the methods side by side: standardised logistic coefficients (his Fig. 1) and the forest’s permutation importance (Fig. 2). The importance here is the average over five forests of 1,000 trees, computed on each tree’s out-of-bag patients as Breiman describes (p. 211).

Code 
def run_importance():
    out = []
    for s in range(5):
        f = B.OOBForest(n_trees=1000, seed=s).fit(Xi, y)
        imp = f.permutation_importance(seed=s)
        out.append({"seed": s, "oob_error": f.oob_error(), **{names[j]: imp[j] for j in range(19)}})
    return pd.DataFrame(out)


imp = cache.frame("hep_importance_v1", run_importance)
imp_mean = imp[names].mean()
imp_rank = imp_mean.sort_values(ascending=False)
lr_perm = cache.obj("lr_perm_v1", lambda: {"v": B.logit_test_permutation(X, y).tolist()})["v"]
lr_top3 = [names[j] for j in np.argsort(lr_perm)[::-1][:3]]
oob_lo, oob_hi = imp["oob_error"].min(), imp["oob_error"].max()
Code 
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.5, 2.9), sharex=True)
hl = [AMBER if j in (ASC, ALB) else PURPLE for j in range(19)]
axes[0].bar(range(1, 20), np.abs(z), color=hl)
axes[0].set_ylabel("|coefficient ÷ s.e.|")
axes[1].bar(range(1, 20), imp_mean.to_numpy(), color=hl)
axes[1].set_ylabel("% rise in OOB error")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xticks(range(1, 20))
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7)
    ax.set_xlabel("covariate (Breiman's numbering)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
  • The forest’s list. Spiders (11), Albumin (17), Protime (18), Ascites (12), in that order. Breiman’s forest singled out 12 and 17. Here albumin is in the top two and ascites is fourth; spiders, which also tops the logistic list, comes first.
  • Logistic regression’s permutation importance, computed the same way on the held-out 10% of each repetition, ranks sex, bilirubin, spiders as its top three. As in Breiman’s check (p. 212), neither 12 nor 17 is among them.
  • The forest’s out-of-bag error is 13.5% to 16.1% over the five seeds.

2.4 Two surrogates

Breiman’s explanation of the Diaconis–Efron finding (p. 212): 12 and 17 are surrogates, so a model built on a bootstrap sample needs only one of them, and each one’s selection frequency is pushed below 50%. He notes that one or the other appears in seven of the ten bootstrap selections Diaconis and Efron list. Efron’s comment adds the full figure from Efron and Gong (1983): 12 or 17 in 60% of bootstrap samples, against 59% for histology (19), the most for any single variable (p. 219).

The selection procedure Gregory used is described only as informal screening followed by an unnamed formal procedure. A forward stepwise logistic regression, adding the variable with the smallest likelihood-ratio p-value while it is below 0.05, stands in for it.

Code 
fwd = cache.obj("forward_boot_v1", lambda: {"picks": B.bootstrap_forward(X, y, boots=500)})["picks"]
fwd_full = B.forward_stepwise_logit(X, y)
f_freq = pd.Series(collections.Counter(j for p in fwd for j in p)).reindex(range(19), fill_value=0) / len(fwd)
f_either = float(np.mean([(ASC in p) or (ALB in p) for p in fwd]))
f_both = float(np.mean([(ASC in p) and (ALB in p) for p in fwd]))
f_sizes = pd.Series([len(p) for p in fwd])
f_top = f_freq.sort_values(ascending=False)
  • On all 155 patients forward selection picks albumin (17), spiders (11), sex (2), bilirubin (14), protime (18), age (1).
  • Over 500 bootstrap resamples it picks between np.int64(2) and np.int64(14) variables, with median 7. The most frequent picks are sex (2) 81%, spiders (11) 74%, bilirubin (14) 67%, albumin (17) 63%.
  • Ascites or albumin is picked in 88% of resamples, both in 12%. Histology (19) is picked in 23%.

The pattern Efron reports holds: the pair together is picked far more often than either member, because a resample rarely needs both. Two numbers differ from his. Histology is picked far less often, and sex far more: all 16 women in the data survived, so in many resamples sex nearly separates the outcome and the likelihood-ratio test reads that as strong evidence. Cox’s comment warns about exactly this, that near-complete separation looks stable when it is not (p. 218).

Code 
f0 = B.OOBForest(n_trees=1000, seed=0).fit(Xi, y)
p_die = f0.oob_proba()[:, 1]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.5, 2.9), sharey=True)
for ax, j, title in [(axes[0], ASC, "ascites (12)"), (axes[1], ALB, "albumin (17)")]:
    v = (Xi[:, j] - Xi[:, j].mean()) / Xi[:, j].std()
    jit = np.random.default_rng(j).uniform(-0.08, 0.08, len(v)) if j == ASC else 0
    ax.scatter(v + jit, p_die, s=10, color=np.where(y == 1, AMBER, TEAL), alpha=0.7, lw=0)
    sm_ = lowess(p_die, v, frac=0.6)
    ax.plot(sm_[:, 0], sm_[:, 1], color=INK, lw=1.6)
    ax.set_xlabel(f"{title}, standardised")
axes[0].set_ylabel("OOB probability of death")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

3 How far to trust permutation importance

Breiman admitted in the rejoinder that importance has no satisfactory theoretical definition and depends on the dependence among the inputs (p. 230). Three later results make that concrete.

  1. Impurity importance is biased toward variables with many split points. The forest’s other built-in measure, total impurity decrease (mean decrease in Gini), credits a continuous or many-category variable for splits that fit noise (Strobl et al. 2007).
  2. Permutation importance shares credit between correlated inputs unevenly. Permuting one input breaks its correlation with the others, so the model is queried at points it never saw. Strobl et al. (2008) propose permuting within strata of the correlated variables instead.
  3. Permuting forces extrapolation. Hooker, Mentch and Zhou (2021) show that the permuted cases fall where there are no data, so the measure reports how the model behaves off the data, not how the data behave. They recommend refitting the model without the variable, or permuting conditionally.

3.1 Design

  • Data. Hepatitis, with two pure-noise columns added: one continuous Gaussian, one binary coded 1/2 like the clinical findings.
  • Measures, each from a forest of 500 trees:
    • impurity (mean decrease in Gini);
    • permutation, Breiman’s out-of-bag measure;
    • conditional permutation of albumin, permuted only among patients with the same ascites value;
    • joint permutation of ascites and albumin together.
  • Replicates. The full data plus 30 bootstrap resamples, each with its own forest.
Code 
reps = cache.frame("importance_reps_v2", lambda: B.importance_replicates(boots=30))
full = reps[reps["boot"] == 0].set_index("var")
mdi_rank = full["mdi"].dropna().rank(ascending=False)
perm_rank = full["perm"].drop("ASCITES+ALBUMIN").rank(ascending=False)
noise_mdi_rank = int(mdi_rank["NOISE_CONT"])
noise_perm = float(full.loc["NOISE_CONT", "perm"])
bin_perm = float(full.loc["NOISE_BIN", "perm"])
bin_mdi_rank = int(mdi_rank["NOISE_BIN"])
alb_perm, alb_cond = float(full.loc["ALBUMIN", "perm"]), float(full.loc["ALBUMIN", "cond"])
asc_perm, pair = float(full.loc["ASCITES", "perm"]), float(full.loc["ASCITES+ALBUMIN", "perm"])
boot = reps[reps["boot"] > 0]
perm_wide = boot[boot["j"] >= 0].pivot(index="boot", columns="var", values="perm")
boot_rank = perm_wide[names].rank(axis=1, ascending=False)
alb_rank_boot, asc_rank_boot = boot_rank["ALBUMIN"], boot_rank["ASCITES"]
# The widget's ranking: all 21 columns, 1 + the number of columns strictly above.
w_rank = perm_wide.rank(axis=1, ascending=False, method="min")
n_swap = int((w_rank["ALBUMIN"] > w_rank["ASCITES"]).sum())
n_split5 = int(((w_rank["ALBUMIN"] <= 5) != (w_rank["ASCITES"] <= 5)).sum())
# Extrapolation: where do permuted albumin values land relative to the real ascites-yes patients?
yes = Xi[:, ASC] == 1
alb_yes_hi = np.quantile(Xi[yes, ALB], 0.9)
perm_alb = np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(Xi[:, ALB])
share_off = float(np.mean(perm_alb[yes] > alb_yes_hi))

3.2 Result

  • Impurity bias. On the full data the continuous noise column ranks 7 of 21 by impurity importance, above most of the clinical findings; the binary noise column ranks 13. Their permutation importances are 0.2% and -0.2% (continuous, binary), near zero, as they should be.
  • Conditional permutation. Permuting albumin freely raises the out-of-bag error by 8.1%; permuting it only within ascites groups raises it by 2.3%. The difference is credit albumin borrows from ascites when the two are pulled apart.
  • The pair. Permuting ascites and albumin together raises the error by 14.5%, against 5.7% and 8.1% separately. This is Breiman’s own point in the rejoinder: delete one of two correlated variables and little changes, delete both and a lot does (p. 230).
  • Resampling. Over 30 bootstrap resamples albumin’s permutation rank among the 19 clinical variables runs from 1 to 16, and ascites’ from 1 to 17. In a resample, out-of-bag means no copy of the patient is in the tree’s bag, so no tree is scored on a patient it was trained on.
  • Extrapolation. Among patients with ascites present, the 90th percentile of albumin is 3.6. After one free permutation of albumin, 70% of those patients are assigned a value above it: ascites with normal albumin, a combination the data contain few of. The permuted forest is being asked about patients who barely exist.
  1. With permutation and resample 0 (the full data), albumin ranks 2 and ascites 3, and the continuous noise column N1 ranks 17 of 21.
  2. Switch to impurity. N1 moves up to 7th, above most of the clinical findings.
  3. Back on permutation, step through resamples 1 to 30. Albumin falls below ascites in 10 of the 30, and in 10 one of them is in the top five while the other is not.

4 Bupa liver disorders

4.1 The class is a train/test flag

Breiman describes the 345 patients as classified into two classes by severity of liver malfunction (p. 212). The current UCI page says the seventh field, “selector”, has been widely misread as a disease label: BUPA’s researchers created it as a train/test selector. McDermott and Forsyth (2016) document the error across hundreds of papers that use the data set as a benchmark, and suggest dichotomising drinks as the target instead.

The paper’s analysis is therefore of the selector. It is re-run here because that is what reproducing it means, and because the result says something about the split.

Code 
bupa = data.bupa()
Xb = bupa[B.BUPA_COLS].to_numpy(float)
yb = bupa["selector"].to_numpy()


def run_bupa():
    out = []
    for s in range(5):
        f = B.OOBForest(n_trees=1000, seed=s).fit(Xb, yb)
        imp = f.permutation_importance(seed=s)
        out.append({"seed": s, "oob_error": f.oob_error(), **{B.BUPA_COLS[j]: imp[j] for j in range(6)}})
    return pd.DataFrame(out)


bres = cache.frame("bupa_v1", run_bupa)
b_err_lo, b_err_hi = bres["oob_error"].min(), bres["oob_error"].max()
b_imp = bres[B.BUPA_COLS].mean().sort_values(ascending=False)
b_base = float(min(np.mean(yb == 1), np.mean(yb == 2)))
fb = B.OOBForest(n_trees=1000, seed=0).fit(Xb, yb)
P = B.proximity(fb, Xb[yb == 2])
D = squareform(1 - P, checks=False)
# Breiman's forests turn proximities into "scaling coordinates" (classical
# multidimensional scaling of 1 - proximity); cluster those with k-means.
nP = len(P)
J = np.eye(nP) - 1 / nP
w_, v_ = np.linalg.eigh(-0.5 * J @ ((1 - P) ** 2) @ J)
coords = v_[:, -3:] * np.sqrt(np.maximum(w_[-3:], 0))
cl = KMeans(2, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(coords) + 1
other = {"Ward linkage": fcluster(linkage(D, "ward"), 2, "maxclust"),
         "spectral clustering": SpectralClustering(2, affinity="precomputed", random_state=0).fit_predict(P),
         "average linkage": fcluster(linkage(D, "average"), 2, "maxclust")}
other_sizes = {k: sorted(pd.Series(v).value_counts().tolist(), reverse=True) for k, v in other.items()}
Zb = (Xb - Xb.mean(0)) / Xb.std(0)
cmeans = pd.DataFrame(Zb[yb == 2], columns=B.BUPA_COLS).groupby(cl).mean()
csize = pd.Series(cl).value_counts().sort_index()
rfr = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=1000, oob_score=True, random_state=0, min_samples_leaf=5)
rfr.fit(Xb[:, :5], bupa["drinks"].to_numpy(float))
drinks_r2 = float(rfr.oob_score_)
  • Error. The forest’s out-of-bag error for the selector is 24.9% to 26.7% over five seeds, against Breiman’s 28%. Guessing the larger group errs on 42.0%.
  • Importance. gammagt 12.1%, sgpt 11.2%, sgot 6.7%, drinks 3.3%. Breiman found blood tests 3 and 5 (sgpt, gammagt) most important, then 4 (sgot) (p. 213); the order here is the same.
  • What that means. The blood tests predict which patients BUPA put in which half of its split, so the split was not random with respect to them. Breiman’s forest found real structure; it was structure in how the data were divided, not in liver disease.
  • The suggested target. A forest predicting drinks from the five blood tests has an out-of-bag of 0.17.

4.2 Clusters within selector 2

Breiman clustered the class-two patients using the forest’s proximities, the share of trees in which two patients land in the same leaf, and found two groups: one high on tests 3, 4 and 5, one low (p. 213). The paper does not say how the clusters were formed. Here the 200 selector-2 patients are placed by classical scaling of , the route Breiman’s forest software used for its “scaling coordinates”, and split in two by k-means: groups of 125 and 75. Ward linkage (105 and 95) and spectral clustering (115 and 85) give similar splits on the same variables. Average linkage does not: it splits off 1 patient and leaves 199 together.

Code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 2.6))
w = 0.38
for k, (c, col) in enumerate(zip(cmeans.index, [PURPLE, TEAL])):
    ax.bar(np.arange(6) + (k - 0.5) * w, cmeans.loc[c].to_numpy(), w, color=col,
           label=f"cluster {k + 1} (n = {int(csize.loc[c])})")
ax.axhline(0, color=MUTED, lw=0.7)
ax.set_xticks(range(6), [f"{j + 1} {c}" for j, c in enumerate(B.BUPA_COLS)])
ax.set_ylabel("mean, standardised")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The two groups separate on tests 3, 4 and 5, as Breiman’s did. With the selector understood, the finding is that the patients BUPA put in one half of its split are a mixture of two blood-test profiles.

5 Lymphoma

Breiman ran a forest on 81 samples with 4,682 genes and no variable selection, and reported that the error rate was low, without a figure (p. 213). The point was that a forest needs no pre-screening of genes and still ranks them.

Code 
Xl, yl = data.lymphoma()


def run_lymph():
    f = B.OOBForest(n_trees=2000, seed=0).fit(Xl, yl)
    imp = f.permutation_importance(seed=0)
    ho = B.holdout({"rf": lambda r: B.rf(r)}, Xl, yl, reps=100)["rf"]
    return {"oob_error": f.oob_error(), "imp": [imp[j] for j in range(Xl.shape[1])],
            "holdout": float(ho.mean()), "holdout_wrong": float((ho > 0).mean())}


lym = cache.obj("lymphoma_v1", run_lymph)
limp = np.array(lym["imp"])
n_pos = int((limp > 0).sum())
top_genes = np.argsort(-limp)[:10] + 1
  • Error. Out-of-bag, 1.2% (one sample of 81). Over 100 random 10% holdouts, 2.8%; 17% of holdouts contain any error at all.
  • Importance. 1,389 of 4,682 genes have positive importance. The ten largest are columns 666, 667, 689, 668, 682, 644, 3531, 3529, 663, 878. Several are adjacent columns, which suggests the file orders genes by some grouping; without gene identifiers that cannot be checked.
Code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 2.4))
ax.vlines(np.arange(1, len(limp) + 1), 0, limp, color=PURPLE, lw=0.6)
ax.set_xlabel("gene (column in Breiman's file)")
ax.set_ylabel("% rise in OOB error")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

6 What the examples show

Breiman drew two conclusions (p. 214): higher predictive accuracy goes with more reliable information about the mechanism, and algorithmic models can give both. The re-runs bear on each.

  • Accuracy as a guard. Hepatitis logistic regression improves on the all-survivor baseline by 4.6 percentage points here, and its coefficient ranking does not survive resampling. That supports his warning: a model this weak should not be read.
  • The forest’s information. The forest’s ranking is not one answer either. On the full data it puts albumin and ascites near the top, but across resamples albumin’s rank drops as low as 16 of 19 and ascites’ as low as 17, and the two share credit in proportions that move with the sample and the measure.
  • What no accuracy reveals. The Bupa forest was accurate about the selector. Accuracy could not reveal that the selector was not the outcome. Cox’s point about knowing what the data mean (Part 5) applies.

7 Constraints

  • Missing values. Breiman does not say how he handled the hepatitis gaps; median imputation inside each training set is one choice, and prothrombin time (67 missing) is the variable it affects most.
  • Forest settings. split candidates and 500–2,000 trees. Breiman’s forest code differed in details (for instance its own missing-value scheme), which may explain part of the smaller gap over logistic regression.
  • Forward selection stands in for Gregory’s procedure, which the sources do not specify.
  • Lymphoma labels are inferred from class counts.

8 Reproduction status

Accuracy. Earns. Attention. Correlation. Splits. Credit. Permutation. Invents. Patients.

9 References

  • Alizadeh, A. A. et al. (2000). Distinct types of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma identified by gene expression profiling. Nature 403(6769), 503–511.
  • Breiman, L. (2001). Random forests. Machine Learning 45, 5–32.
  • Breiman, L. (2001). Statistical modeling: the two cultures (with comments and a rejoinder). Statistical Science 16(3), 199–231.
  • Diaconis, P. & Efron, B. (1983). Computer-intensive methods in statistics. Scientific American 248(5), 116–130.
  • Dudoit, S., Fridlyand, J. & Speed, T. P. (2002). Comparison of discrimination methods for the classification of tumors using gene expression data. Journal of the American Statistical Association 97(457), 77–87.
  • Efron, B. & Gong, G. (1983). A leisurely look at the bootstrap, the jackknife, and cross-validation. The American Statistician 37(1), 36–48.
  • Hooker, G., Mentch, L. & Zhou, S. (2021). Unrestricted permutation forces extrapolation: variable importance requires at least one more model, or there is no free variable importance. Statistics and Computing 31(6), 82.
  • McDermott, J. & Forsyth, R. S. (2016). Diagnosing a disorder in a classification benchmark. Pattern Recognition Letters 73, 41–43.
  • Strobl, C., Boulesteix, A.-L., Zeileis, A. & Hothorn, T. (2007). Bias in random forest variable importance measures: illustrations, sources and a solution. BMC Bioinformatics 8, 25.
  • Strobl, C., Boulesteix, A.-L., Kneib, T., Augustin, T. & Zeileis, A. (2008). Conditional variable importance for random forests. BMC Bioinformatics 9, 307.
  • UCI Machine Learning Repository. Hepatitis and Liver Disorders. CC BY 4.0.
  • The Two Cultures, Part 2: Rashomon — ascites and albumin in perturbed trees and selected models.
  • The Two Cultures, Part 5: The pushback — what importance can mean for a decision.

item.title: The Two Cultures, Part 3: Occam and Bellman
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
Breiman’s second and third lessons say that the most accurate predictors are rarely the simplest, and that adding features, even thousands of them, can make a predictor better rather than worse.

Both run against things most analysts are taught. A model should be as simple as the data allow, and a regression with more variables than cases is a mistake. Yet the classifiers that won benchmark after benchmark in the 1990s were forests of hundreds of trees and support vector machines working in feature spaces of millions of dimensions. Breiman’s sections 9 and 10 take the two observations at face value. This part re-runs his evidence on the same data and then tests the strongest objection to each lesson.

Part 2 covered the first lesson, Rashomon. Part 4 asks what information can be extracted from the complex models this part defends.

This part covers two ideas:

  • Occam. On interpretability a single tree rates an A+ and a forest an F; on prediction it is the other way round (pp. 207–208). The question is whether that trade is forced.
  • Bellman. Instead of reducing dimensionality, increase it by adding many functions of the inputs (p. 208). The question is why that does not overfit.

1 Occam

1.1 The name

William of Ockham (died 1347) was an English Franciscan friar and philosopher. “Occam’s razor” is the principle of parsimony: do not posit more entities than the explanation needs. The phrase came centuries after him, and its best-known wording, “entities must not be multiplied beyond necessity”, is not found in his writings; the idea is attached to him because he used it so often (Simplicity, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy).

Breiman’s version is about prediction, not ontology: simpler is usually taken to mean better, but in prediction accuracy and simplicity are in conflict (p. 206).

1.2 Breiman’s evidence

Table 2 of the paper (p. 207) compares a single CART tree with a random forest on ten classification data sets, mostly from the UCI repository.

  • Five small sets (breast cancer, ionosphere, diabetes, glass, soybean): leave out a random 10%, fit both on the other 90%, score the 10%, repeat 100 times, average.
  • Five large sets (letters, satellite, shuttle, DNA, ZIP-code digits): their own separate test sets.

Breiman’s summary: some errors are halved, others cut by a third (p. 207).

1.3 Data

All ten sets were found in their original form; Table 1 gives the sizes, which match Breiman’s Table 1.

  • Breast cancer (Wisconsin, Wolberg), ionosphere (Johns Hopkins radar returns), glass (forensic glass types), soybean (large soybean, 19 diseases), letters (letter images described by 16 statistics), satellite (Landsat pixels), shuttle (space-shuttle radiator states) and DNA (primate splice junctions): UCI originals; DNA from mlbench, whose row order keeps the original 2,000 / 1,186 split.
  • Diabetes (Pima Indians): from the archived mlbench 2.1-9. UCI no longer distributes this data set, and mlbench dropped it in 2.1-10 following that removal; neither says why. It is used here only because it is in Breiman’s table.
  • Digit: the USPS ZIP-code data, 16 × 16 grey-scale images, from the Elements of Statistical Learning data page.

These are benchmark sets: their purpose was to compare classifiers, and a wrong ranking costs only a misleading table. They suit the comparison because they are the ones Breiman’s readers knew.

1.4 Implementation

  • Single tree. CART grown to purity, then pruned by cost complexity with the size chosen by ten-fold cross-validation on the training data and the one-standard-error rule (Breiman et al. 1984).
  • Forest. 500 trees, variables tried at each split, no tuning.
  • Missing values (breast cancer, soybean): training-median imputation inside each fit.
  • DNA is coded as 180 binary indicators of the 60 nucleotides, as distributed. Breiman’s Table 1 lists 60 variables.
  • Letters has no designated split; the first 15,000 rows train, as the counts in Table 1 imply.
Code 
small = cache.frame("table2_small_v1", lambda: occam.small(reps=100))
large = cache.frame("table2_large_v1", occam.large)
paper = {"Breast cancer": (2.9, 5.9), "Ionosphere": (5.5, 11.2), "Diabetes": (24.2, 25.3),
         "Glass": (22.0, 30.4), "Soybean": (5.7, 8.6), "Letters": (3.4, 12.4),
         "Satellite": (8.6, 14.8), "Shuttle": (0.007, 0.062), "DNA": (3.9, 6.2), "Digit": (6.2, 17.1)}
sizes = {"Breast cancer": "699 / —", "Ionosphere": "351 / —", "Diabetes": "768 / —",
         "Glass": "214 / —", "Soybean": "683 / —", "Letters": "15,000 / 5,000",
         "Satellite": "4,435 / 2,000", "Shuttle": "43,500 / 14,500", "DNA": "2,000 / 1,186",
         "Digit": "7,291 / 2,007"}
s_mean = small.groupby("dataset")[["forest", "tree"]].mean()
s_se = small.groupby("dataset")[["forest", "tree"]].std() / np.sqrt(small["rep"].nunique())
ours = {**{k: (100 * s_mean.loc[k, "forest"], 100 * s_mean.loc[k, "tree"]) for k in s_mean.index},
        **{r["dataset"]: (100 * r["forest"], 100 * r["tree"]) for _, r in large.iterrows()}}
order = list(paper)


def cell(v, k):
    return f"{v:.3f}" if k == "Shuttle" else f"{v:.1f}"


t2 = pd.DataFrame([{"Data set": k, "Train / test": sizes[k],
                    "Forest (Breiman)": cell(paper[k][0], k), "Forest (here)": cell(ours[k][0], k),
                    "Tree (Breiman)": cell(paper[k][1], k), "Tree (here)": cell(ours[k][1], k)}
                   for k in order])
ratio_ours = {k: ours[k][0] / ours[k][1] for k in order}
ratio_paper = {k: paper[k][0] / paper[k][1] for k in order}
shuttle_n = int(large.set_index("dataset").loc["Shuttle", "n_test"])
shuttle_err = {m: int(round(large.set_index("dataset").loc["Shuttle", m] * shuttle_n)) for m in ("forest", "tree")}
max_se = float(100 * s_se.max().max())
min_se = float(100 * s_se.min().min())
md(t2)
Code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.0))
ypos = np.arange(len(order))[::-1]
for yy, k in zip(ypos, order):
    ax.plot([ratio_paper[k], ratio_ours[k]], [yy, yy], color=RULE, lw=2, zorder=1)
ax.scatter([ratio_paper[k] for k in order], ypos, color=AMBER, s=30, label="Breiman (2001)", zorder=2)
ax.scatter([ratio_ours[k] for k in order], ypos, color=PURPLE, s=30, label="re-run", zorder=3)
ax.axvline(0.5, color=MUTED, ls=":", lw=0.8)
ax.axvline(1.0, color=MUTED, ls="--", lw=0.8)
ax.set_yticks(ypos, order)
ax.set_xlabel("forest error ÷ single-tree error")
ax.set_xlim(0, 1.1)
ax.legend(loc="lower right")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

1.5 Reading the table

  • The forest wins on all ten sets, in Breiman’s table and here.
  • Most numbers land within a point or two of his. The holdout means here have standard errors of 0.2 to 0.9 points, and his would have had similar ones, so on the small sets a gap of a point between the two columns is within what two runs of the same method could give.
  • Two rows differ more. DNA (5.4 and 8.5 here, against 3.9 and 6.2) is coded as 180 binary indicators here, not as 60 four-valued variables, and that changes which splits a tree can make. Shuttle’s errors are counts of a handful of cases: 2 and 4 of 14,500 test cases here, against about 1 and 9 implied by his figures.
  • Not reproduced: his ranking of the forest first on all four Statlog sets against the project’s 18 classifiers (p. 208), which needs those classifiers.

1.6 The dilemma, and an objection

Breiman’s conclusion (p. 208): accuracy generally requires more complex prediction methods, so go for accuracy first and try to understand why afterwards. He calls it the Occam dilemma, and later in the paper argues there is no dilemma, because the goal is accurate information rather than interpretability (Part 4).

Hoadley’s comment disputes the premise from credit scoring (pp. 220–224). Fair, Isaac’s segmented scorecards are additive models on binned, engineered characteristics. They are interpretable enough for regulators, and in his experience as accurate as anything else. His Fat Scorecard, a logistic regression on binned dummies of 27 characteristics, slightly beat a neural network with 2,000 weights and held up on test samples one, two and three years later (p. 222). His “Ping-Pong theorem” (p. 223) says a forest could beat any scorecard whose score it was shown, and a scorecard could then beat the forest. The data are proprietary. Rudin (2019) made the same argument general: for structured data with meaningful features, interpretable models that match black boxes usually exist, and high-stakes decisions should use them.

1.7 A scorecard against a forest

1.7.1 Data

  • Source. “Default of credit card clients”, UCI repository, donated by Yeh and Lien (2009): 30,000 credit-card holders in Taiwan with six months of history, April to September 2005; 22% defaulted on the next payment.
  • Inputs. Credit limit, demographics, and six months of repayment status, bill amounts and payment amounts: 23 columns.
  • Why this data. It is the shape of Hoadley’s example, monthly bills and payments over the last months with a default flag as the outcome (p. 220), in public form.
  • Cost of a wrong answer. A bank lends to customers who will not repay, or refuses customers who would.

1.7.2 Models

  1. Logistic regression on the 23 standardised raw columns.
  2. Pruned CART on the raw columns, as in Table 1.
  3. Random forest, 500 trees, minimum leaf size 5, raw columns.
  4. Scorecard. Ten characteristics of the kind Hoadley describes, built from the raw columns: last month’s repayment status, the worst status and the number of late months over six, last-month and six-month utilisation (bill ÷ limit), last-month and six-month payment ratios, the trend in the bill, credit limit and age. Each continuous characteristic is cut into eight quantile bins, the status counts kept as categories, and a logistic regression fitted to the bin indicators.

Each model is fitted on a random two-thirds of clients and scored on the remaining third, for three different splits.

Code 
def run_credit():
    return pd.concat([bellman.credit_models(seed=s)[0].assign(seed=s) for s in (0, 1, 2)])


credit = cache.frame("credit_v1", run_credit)
cg = credit.groupby("model", sort=False).agg(auc_lo=("auc", "min"), auc_hi=("auc", "max"),
                                             err=("error", "mean"), params=("n_params", "median"))
ctab = pd.DataFrame({"Model": cg.index,
                     "Test AUC, three splits": [f"{a:.3f}–{b:.3f}" for a, b in zip(cg["auc_lo"], cg["auc_hi"])],
                     "Test error": [f"{v:.1%}" for v in cg["err"]],
                     "Size": [f"{int(p):,} leaves" if "tree" in m else
                              (f"{int(p):,} nodes" if "forest" in m else f"{int(p)} coefficients")
                              for m, p in zip(cg.index, cg["params"])]})
gap = (credit.pivot(index="seed", columns="model", values="auc")
       .pipe(lambda d: d["Random forest, raw inputs"] - d["Scorecard: logistic on binned characteristics"]))
md(ctab)
  • The scorecard matches the forest. The forest’s AUC minus the scorecard’s is +0.003, -0.001, +0.001 on the three splits.
  • Plain logistic regression is clearly worse, and the pruned tree worse still: the one-standard-error rule cuts it to 2 leaves, one split on whether last month’s payment was two or more months late.
  • None of the four improves much on guessing in raw error, because a 50% threshold is a poor rule when only 22% default; AUC, which ranks clients, is the measure that separates them.

The scorecard’s advantage over plain logistic regression is in its characteristics. Hoadley’s point was not that logistic regression is enough, but that a data-modeling tool with engineered, binned inputs, “linear in an exploded dimension” in his words (p. 221), can be both accurate and readable.

Code 
sc = bellman.credit_scorecard(seed=0)
pre, lr = sc.steps[0][1], sc.steps[-1][1]
names_out = pre.get_feature_names_out()
coef = pd.Series(lr.coef_[0], index=names_out)
status = coef[[n for n in names_out if n.startswith("cats__status_last_")]]
util = coef[[n for n in names_out if n.startswith("bins__util_mean6_")]]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.5, 2.8))
axes[0].bar(range(len(status)), status - status.iloc[0], color=PURPLE)
axes[0].set_xticks(range(len(status)), [n.replace("cats__status_last_", "") for n in status.index], fontsize=7)
axes[0].set_xlabel("last month's repayment status (months late; ≤ 0 on time)")
axes[1].bar(range(len(util)), util - util.iloc[0], color=TEAL)
axes[1].set_xticks(range(len(util)), [str(i + 1) for i in range(len(util))])
axes[1].set_xlabel("six-month utilisation, bin (1 = lowest)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("score weight vs first bin")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

2 Bellman

2.1 The name

“The curse of dimensionality” is Richard Bellman’s phrase, usually credited to his Dynamic Programming (1957): the number of cells needed to cover a space grows exponentially with its dimension. Breiman’s point is the standard advice it produced, reduce the inputs to a few features that “contain most of the information” (p. 208), and his proposal is the opposite: add many functions of the inputs, each carrying a little information, and let the algorithm assemble them.

2.2 Breiman’s evidence

  1. The Amit–Geman shape forest (p. 208): thousands of geometric features, shallow trees choosing among 100 random features per node, over 1,000 trees; 0.7% test error on NIST digits with 100,000 training and 50,000 test images. Not reproduced: the feature hierarchy is not specified in enough detail, and the NIST split is not the public MNIST split.
  2. Support vector machines (pp. 208–209): add all monomials of the inputs up to some degree until the two classes are separated by a hyperplane. On the ZIP-code data, separation came with fourth-degree monomials and a test error of 4.1%.

2.3 Polynomial features on the ZIP-code digits

An SVM with the kernel fits a hyperplane in the space of all monomials of the 256 pixels up to degree , without forming them. Here , the cost parameter is so the margin is effectively hard, and the ten classes are handled one pair at a time.

Code 
svm = cache.frame("svm_v1", bellman.svm_degrees)
stab = pd.DataFrame({"Degree d": svm["degree"],
                     "Features": [f"{v:,}" for v in svm["n_features"]],
                     "Training error": [f"{v:.1%}" for v in svm["train_error"]],
                     "Test error": [f"{v:.1%}" for v in svm["test_error"]],
                     "Support vectors": [f"{v:,}" for v in svm["support_vectors"]],
                     "Support vectors ÷ (N − 1)": [f"{v / 7290:.1%}" for v in svm["support_vectors"]]})
svm4 = svm.set_index("degree").loc[4]
md(stab)
  • Every degree separates the training set, including degree 1: with 256 pixels and a few hundred images per digit, each pair of digits is linearly separable. Breiman’s “separation occurs with fourth degree monomials” (p. 209) does not hold here in the one-pair-at-a-time sense; he does not say how the multi-class problem was set up.
  • Test error falls with degree, from 7.4% at to 5.2% at , against his 4.1%. At the hyperplane lives in a space of 186,043,584 dimensions, fitted to 7,291 images.
  • Vapnik’s bound (p. 209) says the expected error is at most the expected number of support vectors divided by . Read loosely for the multi-class machine, that is about 26% at degree 4: true, and five times the observed error.

The bound grows with the number of support vectors, not with the dimension, which is why a space of 186 million dimensions need not overfit. It explains why the curse can be lifted; it does not predict the error.

2.4 Past the interpolation threshold

Efron’s comment asks where the bias went (p. 219): a model with more knobs than data points must be a biased estimator, or it could not predict. A later line of work gives one answer for least squares. Belkin, Hsu, Ma and Mandal (2019) showed that as a model’s size passes the number of training points, test error first rises to a peak, where the model can just fit the data, and then falls again. Among the many fits that interpolate the data, the fitting procedure picks the one of smallest norm, and that choice is the bias Efron was looking for. They call the curve double descent.

2.4.1 Design

  • Data. 1,000 USPS training digits drawn at random, the full 2,007-image test set.
  • Features. random ReLU features of the 256 pixels, with Gaussian, for from 10 to 20,000.
  • Fit. Least squares from the features to one-hot digit labels; minimum-norm solution when . A second series adds a small ridge penalty, .
  • Replicates. Five draws of the training digits and of .
Code 
rf0 = cache.frame("randfeat_v1", lambda: bellman.random_features())
rf1 = cache.frame("randfeat_ridge_v1", lambda: bellman.random_features(ridge=1e-1))
c0 = rf0.groupby("width")[["train_error", "test_error"]].mean()
c1 = rf1.groupby("width")[["train_error", "test_error"]].mean()
classic = c0[c0.index < 1000]["test_error"]
classic_w, classic_e = int(classic.idxmin()), float(classic.min())
near = c0[(c0.index > 500) & (c0.index < 2000)]["test_error"]
peak_w, peak_e = int(near.idxmax()), float(near.max())
end_e = float(c0["test_error"].iloc[-1])
ridge_peak = float(c1[(c1.index > 500) & (c1.index < 2000)]["test_error"].max())
interp_w = int(c0[c0["train_error"] < 0.001].index.min())
Code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.0))
for c, col, lab in [(c0, PURPLE, "minimum norm"), (c1, TEAL, "ridge λ = 0.1")]:
    ax.plot(c.index, c["test_error"], color=col, lw=1.8, label=f"test, {lab}")
    ax.plot(c.index, c["train_error"], color=col, lw=1.0, ls="--")
ax.axvline(1000, color=MUTED, ls=":", lw=0.8)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("random features p")
ax.set_ylabel("misclassification")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

2.4.2 Result

  • The classical curve. Test error falls to 13.6% at 334 features and then rises, the textbook picture of overfitting.
  • The peak. Training error is below 0.1% from 493 features on. Test error peaks at 45.0% at 1,075 features, just past . There the features can only just fit the 1,000 labels, the coefficients needed to do it are large (their norm peaks near ), and the fit swings wildly between training points.
  • The second descent. At 20,000 features test error is 8.2%, below the classical minimum.
  • Regularisation removes the peak. With the highest test error near is 22.5%.
  1. The slider starts at 334 features, near the classical minimum: test error 13.6%.
  2. Move to 1,075. Training error is 0%; test error is 45.0%.
  3. Move to 20,000. Both curves are low: 8.2% test error with zero training error.
  4. Switch to the ridge fit at 1,075. The peak shrinks to 19.5%.

Breiman’s Bellman lesson was empirical: more features helped. Double descent is one mechanism behind it, for one family of models. It does not cover forests, whose averaging is a different kind of regularisation (Breiman 2001).

3 Constraints

  • Implementations differ from 2001. scikit-learn’s CART pruning and forest are not Breiman’s Fortran; the tree’s pruning rule and the forest’s settings are stated in Section 1.4 and were not tuned to match his figures.
  • One scorecard, one data set. The credit result supports Hoadley’s existence claim, that an interpretable model can match a forest on some data; it does not show that one always exists.
  • The SVM setup is a choice. , the cost and the one-pair-at-a-time scheme were fixed in advance. Tuning them on held-out folds would likely lower the error toward published figures near 4%, but that is a different experiment from Breiman’s.
  • Double descent here is for least squares on random features. It is a demonstration of a mechanism, not an account of why forests or SVMs generalise.

4 Reproduction status

Forests. Win. Scorecards. Tie. Dimensions. Help. When. Norms. Stay. Small.

5 References

  • Amit, Y. & Geman, D. (1997). Shape quantization and recognition with randomized trees. Neural Computation 9(7), 1545–1588.
  • Simplicity. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
  • Belkin, M., Hsu, D., Ma, S. & Mandal, S. (2019). Reconciling modern machine-learning practice and the classical bias–variance trade-off. PNAS 116(32), 15849–15854.
  • Bellman, R. (1957). Dynamic Programming. Princeton University Press.
  • Breiman, L. (2001). Random forests. Machine Learning 45, 5–32.
  • Breiman, L. (2001). Statistical modeling: the two cultures (with comments and a rejoinder). Statistical Science 16(3), 199–231.
  • Breiman, L., Friedman, J. H., Olshen, R. A. & Stone, C. J. (1984). Classification and Regression Trees. Wadsworth.
  • Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R. & Friedman, J. (2009). The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed. Springer. Source of the USPS ZIP-code data files.
  • Leisch, F. & Dimitriadou, E. mlbench: Machine Learning Benchmark Problems, R package, versions 2.1-9 (Pima) and 2.1-11 (DNA).
  • Rudin, C. (2019). Stop explaining black box machine learning models for high stakes decisions and use interpretable models instead. Nature Machine Intelligence 1(5), 206–215.
  • Vapnik, V. (1995). The Nature of Statistical Learning Theory. Springer.
  • Yeh, I.-C. & Lien, C.-H. (2009). The comparisons of data mining techniques for the predictive accuracy of probability of default of credit card clients. Expert Systems with Applications 36(2), 2473–2480.
  • The Two Cultures, Part 2: Rashomon — Hoadley’s Fat Scorecard as a Rashomon set.
  • The Two Cultures, Part 4: Information from a black box — extracting information from the complex models.

item.title: The Two Cultures, Part 2: Rashomon, or Many Equally Good Models
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
A fitted model that explains the data well is usually one of many that explain it about as well, and those models can disagree about which inputs matter.

Anyone who has run stepwise regression twice, on last year’s data and then this year’s, has seen this. The fit barely changes and the list of “significant” variables does. The usual reading is that the second run found the truth or the first one did. Breiman’s reading, in section 8 of The Two Cultures, is that neither did: the data never picked one model, and the procedure picked one at random from a crowd.

Part 1 set out Breiman’s two cultures and re-ran his ozone forecast. This part tests his first lesson from machine learning on data close to his own. Part 3 takes the second and third.

This part covers two ideas:

  • The Rashomon effect. Many models with different structure have nearly the same error, and each tells a different story about the inputs.
  • Instability and its repair. A procedure that picks one model from such a crowd jumps between them when the data change slightly. Averaging over the crowd (bagging) gives up the single story and recovers accuracy.

1 The name

Rashomon is Akira Kurosawa’s 1950 film, built from two stories by Ryūnosuke Akutagawa, “In a Grove” and “Rashōmon”. In Breiman’s summary, four witnesses to a death in a forest report the same facts and tell very different stories about what happened. His statistical version (p. 206): in a class of functions there is often a multitude of different descriptions, all with about the same minimum error.

He gives three examples:

  1. Subsets. With 30 variables there are about 140,000 five-variable regressions, and generally many have residual sum of squares within 1% of the lowest. He prints three on disjoint variables, each telling a different story (p. 206).
  2. Trees. Removing a random 2–3% of the training set can give a quite different tree with almost the same test error (p. 206).
  3. Networks. A small net run 100 times on simple three-dimensional data from small random starting weights found 32 distinct minima, each a different picture, with about equal test error (p. 206).

The three equations he prints are illustrations, and the data behind all three examples are not given. Each is re-run here on public data close to his.

2 Data

  • 1976 Los Angeles ozone (mlbench::Ozone), as in Part 1: next-day maximum ozone from days , and of eight meteorological readings and ozone, plus season and a weekend flag. That makes 30 candidate predictors, the count in Breiman’s subset example. Training January–August (189 day pairs), test September–December (93). Ozone is a forecasting problem of the kind he worked on, and its predictors are correlated the way weather is, which is what makes many subsets compete.
  • Hepatitis (UCI, contributed by Gail Gong): 155 patients, 19 covariates, 32 deaths. Breiman’s own example in section 11; Part 4 reproduces his analysis. Its small size and correlated laboratory values are the conditions under which a tree or a variable list is unstable, and its users wanted a short list of prognostic variables, which is the output that instability corrupts.

Sources, licences and checksums are in the series’ data/README.md.

3 Five-variable regressions

3.1 Every subset

There are five-variable regressions. Fitting them all takes a fraction of a second: each fit needs only a block of the Gram matrix , and the blocks are solved as one batch.

Code 
names, fits = rashomon_exp.ozone_subsets()
ratio = fits["rss"] / fits["rss"].min()
test = fits["test_mse"]
counts = {t: int((ratio <= 1 + t).sum()) for t in (0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.05, 0.10)}
oz_in = names.index("ozone_lag0")
w5 = ratio <= 1.05
share_oz_5 = float(np.isin(fits["idx"][w5], [oz_in]).any(1).mean())
best = int(np.argmin(ratio))
best_test = int(np.argmin(test))
w3 = ratio <= 1.03
t3_lo, t3_hi = float(test[w3].min()), float(test[w3].max())
inc3 = np.array([np.isin(fits["idx"][w3], [j]).any(1).mean() for j in range(len(names))])
always3 = [names[j] for j in np.flatnonzero(inc3 == 1)]
rank_of_best_on_test = int((test < test[best]).sum()) + 1
  • Within 1% of the lowest training RSS: 4 models. Breiman says there are generally many; on 189 training days there are few.
  • Within 2%, 3%, 5% and 10%: 15, 42, 175 and 2,886 models.
  • Today’s ozone is in 100% of the models within 5%. The disagreement is about the meteorology.
  • On the test months, the models within 3% have test MSE from 24.5 to 29.2. The model with the lowest training RSS ranks 12,533 of 142,506 on test error.
Code 
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.5, 3.0))
ax = axes[0]
ax.hist(np.minimum(ratio, 2), bins=100, color=PURPLE, log=True)
ax.set_xlabel("training RSS ÷ best")
ax.set_ylabel("subsets")
ax = axes[1]
w10 = ratio <= 1.10
ax.scatter(ratio[w10], test[w10], s=4, color=TEAL, alpha=0.5, lw=0)
ax.scatter([ratio[best]], [test[best]], s=30, color=AMBER, zorder=3, label="lowest training RSS")
for t in (0.01, 0.03, 0.05):
    ax.axvline(1 + t, color=MUTED, ls="--", lw=0.7)
ax.set_xlabel("training RSS ÷ best")
ax.set_ylabel("test MSE (Sep–Dec)")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

3.2 Three pictures

Breiman’s three pictures share no variables. The three here are picked from the models within 5% so that each overlaps the others as little as possible. They cannot be disjoint, because all of them keep today’s ozone.

Code 
order = np.where(w5)[0][np.argsort(ratio[w5])]
picked = []
for _ in range(3):
    best_i, best_ov = None, 99
    for i in order:
        if i in picked:
            continue
        ov = sum(len(set(fits["idx"][i]) & set(fits["idx"][j])) for j in picked)
        if ov < best_ov:
            best_i, best_ov = i, ov
    picked.append(best_i)


def equation(i):
    terms = [f"{'+' if b >= 0 else '−'} {abs(b):.2g}·{nice(names[j])}" for j, b in zip(fits["idx"][i], fits["coef"][i])]
    return f"{fits['intercept'][i]:.1f} " + " ".join(terms)


pics = pd.DataFrame([{"Picture": k + 1, "RSS ÷ best": f"{ratio[i]:.3f}",
                      "Test MSE": f"{test[i]:.1f}", "Equation": equation(i)}
                     for k, i in enumerate(picked)])
pic_vars = [set(nice(names[j]) for j in fits["idx"][i]) for i in picked]
md(pics)
  • Picture 1 forecasts from the inversion layer: its height and temperature at LAX today, plus a pressure gradient and an older temperature.
  • Picture 2 forecasts from the season, the upper air (500 mb height) and today’s pressure gradient, with no inversion height at all.
  • Picture 3 forecasts mostly from ozone itself, three days of it, plus today’s temperature and an inversion temperature from two days back.

A meteorologist reading one picture would learn something different from one reading another. The data do not choose between them.

3.3 Explorer

  1. At the starting tolerance of 1.0%, the tiles read 4 models using 9 different variables.
  2. Drag the tolerance to 3.0%. There are 42 models, and between them they use all 30 variables. Their test MSE runs from 24.5 to 29.2.
  3. Drag it to 10%. The inclusion bars flatten: apart from today’s ozone, no variable is in more than half the qualifying models.

4 Trees

4.1 Design

  • Data. Hepatitis, with a fixed random 30% of patients held out for testing (46 patients, 10 deaths) and missing values filled with training medians.
  • Model. CART with cost-complexity pruning, size chosen by ten-fold cross-validation with the one-standard-error rule, as in Breiman et al. (1984).
  • Perturbation. Remove a random 3% of the 109 training patients (3 patients), refit, repeat 100 times.
Code 
tree_rows, tree_info = (lambda o: (o["rows"], o["info"]))(cache.obj(
    "trees_v2", lambda: dict(zip(["rows", "info"], rashomon_exp.tree_perturbations(reps=100)))))
tr = pd.DataFrame([{k: v for k, v in r.items() if k != "structure"} for r in tree_rows])
pert = tr[tr["rep"] > 0]
root_counts = pert["root"].value_counts()
sig_counts = pert["signature"].value_counts()
base_err = float(tr.loc[tr["rep"] == 0, "test_error"].iloc[0])
err_lo, err_hi = float(pert["test_error"].min()), float(pert["test_error"].max())
n_sig = int(pert["signature"].nunique())
n_stump = int(root_counts.get("leaf", 0))
split = pert[pert["root"] != "leaf"]
base_rate = tree_info["test_deaths"] / tree_info["n_test"]
split_lo, split_hi = float(split["test_error"].min()), float(split["test_error"].max())

4.2 Result

  • No split at all. The tree fitted to the full training set splits first on ascites. In 45 of the 100 perturbed fits the one-standard-error rule prunes the tree back to its root: on about 106 patients, predicting that everyone lives is within one standard error of the best cross-validated tree.
  • Root split, when there is one. Ascites 39 times and albumin 14 times; the rest go to bilirubin or prothrombin time.
  • Structure. Counting the root-only tree, the top two levels take 9 different forms.
  • Test error. 17.4% for the unperturbed tree. The root-only trees all score 21.7%, the share of the 46 test patients who died; trees with a split range from 15.2% to 23.9%. On 46 test patients one misclassification is 2.2 points: the best tree with a split gets 3 more patients right than predicting survival for everyone, and the worst gets 1 fewer.
Code 
top = sig_counts.index[:7]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.5, 3.0), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.3, 1]})
ax = axes[0]
labels = ["root only" if s == "leaf" else s.replace("SPLEEN_PALPABLE", "SPLEEN").replace(" / ", " │ ")
          for s in top]
ax.barh(range(len(top))[::-1], sig_counts[top].to_numpy(), color=PURPLE)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(top))[::-1], labels, fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlabel("perturbed fits")
ax = axes[1]
