Smallest instance: , phase retrieval. , so and least squares learns nothing; , so and its top eigenvector is .

  • Odd links have and even links , so each moment estimator is blind to one family.
  • Information exponent 3, as for , defeats both: the first nonzero moment is a third-order tensor, in the multivariate Hermite basis. Ben Arous et al. (2021) show that online SGD from a random start then needs a number of samples growing like , up to logarithmic factors, for information exponent , against for .

3.2 One gradient step

Train on squared loss, with the first-layer weights started at zero. At , is the constant , so , and the gradient of in is

One step of gradient descent moves every hidden unit along . With samples it moves them along , the first-order Stein estimate. When the step moves the units along noise, and the direction can only enter through higher-order terms: from a small random start , the next term of brings in , the second moment of Equation 4 acting on (for centred ). Ba et al. (2022) show that one gradient step from a random start adds a rank-one spike along the target direction to the first-layer weights, with a size set by the linear (first Hermite) components of the target and the activation. Damian, Lee & Soltanolkotabi (2022) remove the linear part of first; their first step is then driven by the second-order term and recovers the subspace the target depends on.

3.3 Two estimators on synthetic data

The data are synthetic. Inputs are , the hidden direction is a fixed unit vector , and is the link , standardised to mean 0 and variance 1, plus noise. The setting stands in for a regression whose target depends on one unknown combination of many features, the simplest case of feature learning. A wrong answer is a probe that reports no linear signal in a feature that the target depends on.

The chart shows the link’s Hermite coefficients and, against sample size, the overlap between and two estimates: the first-order , and the top eigenvector (largest absolute eigenvalue) of . Lines are means over six data sets and bands their range.

Things to try:

  1. Defaults (ReLU, , , ). Both coefficients are nonzero, and both estimates find : overlaps 0.96 and 0.88. Over 30 data sets the first-order estimate passes 0.9 at and the second-order one at .
  2. tanh. . The first-order overlap reaches 0.99 by . The second-order one stays between 0.27 and 0.37 at every from 25 to 12,800, averaged over 30 data sets; in the chart it wanders between about 0.24 and 0.43 and never rises. Its population matrix is zero, so it estimates noise.
  3. or . Now . The roles swap: the second-order overlap reaches 0.98 to 0.99 by , and the first-order one, averaged over 30 data sets, stays between 0.20 and 0.33 at every (the chart’s six data sets dip to 0.16).
  4. Dimension. For ReLU, averaged over 30 data sets, the at which the first-order overlap passes 0.9 is 100, 200 and 400 at , 20 and 40, and for the second-order estimate 400, 800 and 1600. Both scale linearly in , with the second order needing four times as many samples.
  5. Noise. Over the slider’s range, label noise adds no more error than the randomness of itself; at the two contribute equally. For ReLU at and , averaged over 30 data sets, the first-order overlap is 0.90 at and 0.82 at . The chart’s first six data sets read 0.89 and 0.85.
  6. The floor. A blind estimate need not sit at , the dashed line, which is the root-mean-square overlap of a uniformly random direction. For the linear link at the second-order overlap, averaged over 30 data sets, levels off between 0.46 and 0.55 from on (the chart reads 0.44 to 0.56), against . Its noise is not isotropic: with and , the off-diagonal entries in the row and column of are times noisier than the rest, and the diagonal entry at is times noisier than the other diagonal entries, so even a zero-mean estimate leans toward . It never approaches 1.

4 The series in machine learning

Each tool in the series has an established use in machine learning. Each row names the part that derives the tool and cites a paper that introduced or analysed the use; the two rows about this part point to its sections.

Part Tool Use in machine learning
1 Gaussian integration by parts The gradient of a Gaussian-smoothed objective is an average of function values, for : the evolution-strategies estimator used to train neural-network policies without backpropagation (Salimans et al. 2017). Part 4 gave the score-function and reparameterisation version for policy gradients.
1, 4 SURE Training denoisers without clean data (Soltanayev & Chun 2018, in Part 4). Its Bayesian counterpart, Tweedie’s formula for with marginal density , links denoising to the score (Efron 2011).
2, 6 Normal approximation Width corrections to the Gaussian-process limit of random networks (Section 2).
3 Kernel Stein discrepancy Goodness-of-fit tests against an unnormalised model (Liu, Lee & Jordan 2016; Chwialkowski, Strathmann & Gretton 2016) and sample-quality checks; the anti-collapse regulariser of Nuisance Leakage in JEPA Embeddings, and a training regulariser in general (Part 7).
3 SVGD Posterior inference for Bayesian neural networks (Liu & Wang 2016), policy exploration (Liu et al. 2017), and ensembles with a kernel repulsion between members (D’Angelo & Fortuin 2021).
4 Score matching Denoising score matching (Vincent 2011), the training objective of score-based diffusion models (Song & Ermon 2019).
5 Poisson equation The bias and fluctuations of stochastic-gradient Langevin dynamics (Teh, Thiery & Vollmer 2016), and zero-variance control variates for posterior expectations (Mira, Solgi & Imparato 2013).
6 Hermite coefficients Which directions gradient descent can learn, and how many samples it needs (Section 3).

5 Constraints

  • One input, one hidden layer. Corollary 2 is for one output at one input of a one-hidden-layer network. Two inputs need a multivariate normal approximation, and deeper networks need control of the dependent terms in , which the cited papers supply.
  • Gaussian output weights. With Rademacher output weights the output is not a Gaussian scale mixture, and Proposition 1 does not apply. Part 2’s Theorem 4 still does.
  • Constants. Equation 2 is 8.5 times the true large-width distance for every activation. The rate and the dependence on are right; the factor is lost in the Taylor step of Proposition 1.
  • Gaussian inputs. Equation 4 needs Gaussian . Other input laws need the score in Equation 3, which has to be known or estimated, for example by Part 4’s score matching.
  • Blind spots. Moment estimators of order 1 and 2 cannot see a link of information exponent 3 or more, and their noise floors need not sit at (item 6).
  • One step. Section 3 describes the first gradient step, not training. Later steps change the network’s output, so no longer vanishes.

6 Next in the series

  • Part 7: Part 3’s kernel Stein discrepancy as a training regulariser for the codes of a VAE and the embeddings of a JEPA, and what its kernel lets it see in 64 dimensions.

Widths. Set. Gaussianity. Hermite. Coefficients. Set. Directions. Stein. Measures. Both.

item.title: Stein’s Method, Part 5: Markov Chain Monte Carlo
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
A Markov chain built to sample a density comes with its own Stein operator, and the Stein equation for that operator is the chain’s Poisson equation. One solution of it gives the bias of an approximate sampler such as unadjusted Langevin, the variance of an exact sampler’s averages, and the control variate that would remove that variance.

Every MCMC run fixes a step size and a number of iterations, and both trade accuracy for cost in ways a trace plot does not show. A larger step lowers the autocorrelation. In a sampler without a Metropolis correction it also moves the chain’s long-run distribution away from the target, and no between-chain diagnostic sees that shift, because every chain shifts the same way. Part 3 measured the shift after the run with a kernel Stein discrepancy. Part 2 had a sharper tool in reserve: the Stein equation, whose solution converts a difference of expectations into an expectation under one law. For a Markov chain the same equation sizes the bias and the variance at once.

Part 1 built the Langevin Stein operator. Part 2 solved the Stein equation and noted Barbour’s generator approach in one line; this part runs it. Part 3 audited MCMC output with the kernel Stein discrepancy and built Stein control variates for independent samples. Part 4 fitted unnormalised models. Part 6 turns to neural networks, and Part 7 to training regularisers.

An AI agent (Claude) drafted the text and the interactive charts. Separate review passes checked each derivation numerically and each reference against its source.

Three ideas carry the post:

  1. Markov kernels are Stein operators. If a kernel leaves invariant, for every integrable . The generator of the Langevin diffusion is the Langevin Stein operator applied to gradients, and the Stein equation becomes the Poisson equation.
  2. Bias is a mismatch of operators. An unadjusted sampler’s stationary law satisfies its own kernel’s identity, not the target’s. Evaluating the difference on the Poisson solution gives the bias, first order in the step size for unadjusted Langevin.
  3. Variance comes from the same solution. The Poisson solution sets the asymptotic variance of an exact sampler, and subtracting the generator applied to an approximation of it is a zero-variance control variate.

1 Notation

  • : the target density on , positive and smooth; its score; an unnormalised version.
  • : a Markov chain with transition kernel , acting on functions by .
  • is invariant for if implies .
  • Langevin diffusion: , with a standard Brownian motion. Its generator is .
  • ULA (unadjusted Langevin algorithm): with and step size . Its kernel is and its stationary law .
  • MALA (Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm): the ULA move as a proposal, accepted with the Metropolis–Hastings probability.
  • : a test function; .
  • : the MCMC estimate of .
  • : the asymptotic variance, the limit of .
  • : the solution of the Stein equation, as in Part 2.

2 Markov kernels as Stein operators

Part 1 built a Stein operator by integration by parts. A second construction needs no calculus.

Proposition 1 — a kernel’s Stein identity

  • The operator. is a Stein operator for : its outputs have mean zero under .
  • The Stein equation. For a test function it reads . With this is , the Poisson equation of the chain.
  • No normalising constant. A Metropolis–Hastings kernel uses only through ratios , so the operator never sees , like the Langevin operator of Part 1.

Smallest instance: an independence sampler that ignores the current state and draws . Then for every , and Equation 1 is .

2.1 The Langevin generator

In continuous time the kernel becomes a generator, , where moves the diffusion forward by time . By Itô’s formula the Langevin diffusion has generator .

Proposition 2 — the generator and the Poisson equation

Let be positive and continuously differentiable, and let be twice continuously differentiable. Then

In one dimension, let . Every solution of with as has , where

Proof.

  1. Operator. , so is the Langevin operator at . The product rule and give .
  2. One dimension. reads . Integrating from , where , gives .
  • The name. The Langevin Stein operator of Part 1 is the generator of the Langevin diffusion acting on gradient fields. Barbour’s generator approach (Part 2) picks a process with stationary law and uses its generator as the Stein operator.
  • Part 2 is the Gaussian case. For the diffusion is the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, . With , the Poisson equation is Part 2’s Stein equation , and Equation 3 is Part 2’s solution with the integrating factor replaced by .

3 The bias of unadjusted Langevin

ULA is the Euler discretisation of the Langevin diffusion. It has no accept step. When it is ergodic its kernel leaves a law invariant, and ; for some targets whose score grows faster than linearly it is not ergodic at all (Roberts & Tweedie 1996). The long-run average converges to , not to . Stein’s method compares the two operators.

Proposition 3 — bias as a mismatch of operators

Let have invariant law , and let solve with and finite. Then

Proof.

  1. Evaluate the Poisson equation under . .
  2. Subtract a zero. Proposition 1 for and gives . Subtract times it.

The structure is Part 2’s. There, became an expectation under of the target’s Stein operator applied to the Stein solution. Here , and the sampler’s law satisfies its own kernel’s identity exactly, so only the difference of the two operators survives.

Smallest instance: and , so . ULA is the autoregression , and

Equation 4 becomes for the stationary variance , so and the bias is , exactly.

3.1 First order in the step size

In general has no closed form, but a Taylor expansion in does.

Theorem 4 — first-order bias of ULA in one dimension

Let be positive on with a score that is three times continuously differentiable, and let be such that the Taylor expansion and the integrations by parts in the derivation are justified, with remainders . Then

Derivation.

  1. Expand the kernel. One ULA step moves by , with , , and . Taylor’s theorem gives

  2. Insert into Equation 4. The bias is . Since , the expectation can be taken under at the same order.

  3. Remove the higher derivatives. Write . Part 1’s identity with gives . With it gives . Substituting both, , which is the first form.

  4. Remove . The Stein equation gives , so . Part 1’s identity with gives

    So , the second form.

The order of the bias for smooth goes back to the expansion of Talay & Tubaro (1990) (Durmus & Moulines 2017, Remark 11), and Mattingly, Stuart & Tretyakov (2010) make Poisson-equation arguments of this kind rigorous for time averages of SDE discretisations on the torus. The derivation here is the formal version, checked numerically in Section 3.3.

Three readings:

  • The density. Equation 5 holds for every , so to first order . ULA over-weights wherever is large. For a log-concave target with a Lipschitz score that is the tails, where is large, so ULA’s stationary law is too wide.
  • Smallest instance. For , , and , so the bias in is , the first term of .
  • dimensions. The same expansion gives . For that is , the first-order correction to the Euler–Maruyama invariant density that Leimkuhler, Matthews & Stoltz (2016, Theorem 2.10) derive on the torus. For the bias in is , or per coordinate.

MALA removes the bias. Its accept step makes satisfy detailed balance with , so is invariant and Proposition 3 gives zero. The price is rejections, which can raise the variance at large steps. Within the chart’s range only the two-mode target shows it: at MALA accepts 83% of proposals, and its asymptotic variance for the mean is 1.8 times ULA’s.

3.2 Bias against variance

An average over ULA steps has mean squared error for large .

  • Bias grows like , with from Equation 5.
  • Variance. steps of size cover diffusion time , so , where is the diffusion’s asymptotic variance (Section 4).
  • Optimum. is smallest at . There the mean squared error is , which falls like .

So the root mean squared error of a tuned ULA average falls like , against for an exact sampler. Teh, Thiery & Vollmer (2016) prove the same rate for the mean squared error of stochastic-gradient Langevin dynamics with decreasing step sizes, by a Poisson-equation argument.

3.3 ULA and MALA on three targets

The targets are synthetic one-dimensional densities. Each stands in for a posterior shape:

  • Gaussian: , the large-sample posterior of a regular model. Every quantity has a closed form.
  • Heavier tails: , Gaussian near the centre with exponential tails, like a robust-regression posterior.
  • Two modes: , like a posterior with two explanations of the data.

A wrong answer here means a posterior summary that is off by more than its Monte Carlo error suggests.

The chart computes everything without simulation. Each sampler’s transition kernel is discretised on a grid of 241 points, so its stationary law is a left eigenvector and its asymptotic variance the solution of the discrete Poisson equation (Section 4). Both come from one LU factorisation. A grid of 481 points changes no nonzero bias by more than 0.04%. An independent numpy implementation of the same computation draws Figure 1.

The chart shows ULA’s stationary density minus the target density, and the error of an -step average against step size for both samplers.

Things to try:

  1. Defaults (Gaussian, second moment, , ). ULA’s bias is 0.0526, the exact , and Stein’s first-order prediction is 0.0500. In the left panel ULA’s density minus the target’s is negative at the centre and positive in both tails, so its stationary law is too wide, and the dashed first-order prediction sits almost on it.
  2. Shrink the step. At the bias is 0.00503 against a prediction of 0.00500, a ratio of 1.005. At the ratio is 1.25: the prediction is first order only.
  3. Raise the budget. ULA’s best step, circled on its curve, is 0.148 at , 0.070 at , 0.033 at and 0.016 at . Each tenfold increase in shrinks it by about 2.1 and its error by 2.17 to 2.22, close to . MALA’s best step stays at the slider’s end, 0.4, for every target and estimate, and its error falls by per decade. At the error at each best step is 0.0138 for ULA and 0.00207 for MALA.
  4. Two modes, mean. Stein’s coefficient is . The ratio of exact bias to prediction is 1.033 at , 1.33 at 0.1 and 2.43 at 0.4. Between the modes rises to , where is convex, so the expansion needs a smaller step than on the Gaussian.
  5. Tail probability. On the Gaussian, and . At ULA’s bias is 0.00288, so it reports 0.0257, 13% too high, because is largest in the tails. An indicator is not smooth enough for the derivation of Theorem 4, but the grid confirms its covariance form: the ratio is 1.006 at .
  6. Mean on a symmetric target. On the Gaussian and the heavier-tailed target the bias in the mean is zero at every step, because the target is symmetric and ULA’s step preserves the symmetry. is even, so Stein’s coefficient is zero too. Only the variance term remains, and both samplers’ errors fall as the step grows.

4 The variance of an exact sampler

MALA has no bias, so its error is variance alone. The variance of a Markov chain average is not : neighbouring states are correlated. The Poisson solution measures how much.

Discrete time. For an ergodic chain started at ,

The series , when it converges, solves , and

The chart computes this for both samplers.

Continuous time. For the Langevin diffusion the same quantity has a cleaner form.

Proposition 5 — asymptotic variance from the Poisson solution

Let the Langevin diffusion be started at , let solve , and assume , , and boundary terms that vanish. Then

In one dimension this is : twice the mean square of the Stein solution.

Derivation.

  1. Covariances. The limit is

  2. Integrate the semigroup. , so . The limit is , since .

  3. Integrate by parts. By Equation 2, , so

  • Smallest instance. and : , so the limit is 2. Directly, the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck autocorrelation is , and .
  • Steps of size . steps cover time , so a Langevin-type chain has for small . On the chart’s grid at , Equation 6 is within 1.1% of it for both samplers, every target and every estimate.
  • Slow mixing is a large Stein solution. For the mean, is 2.0 for the Gaussian, 11.7 for the two-mode target and 16.2 for the heavier tails. Part 2 bounded the size of the Stein solution to bound a distance; here its size is the variance.

4.1 Zero-variance control variates

Proposition 2 makes a function with mean zero under for any suitable . Subtracting it from leaves the mean unchanged. With it leaves the constant : an estimate with zero variance. Assaraf & Caffarel (1999) introduced this zero-variance principle in quantum Monte Carlo, and Mira, Solgi & Imparato (2013) brought it to Bayesian MCMC.

Proposition 6 — what a control variate leaves

Under the conditions of Proposition 5 for and for ,

where is the limit in Equation 7.

Proof. , so has mean , and its centred version is . Its Poisson solution is . Apply Proposition 5.

A control variate for MCMC is therefore an approximate solution of the Stein equation, scored by the error in its gradient.

  • Polynomials. Mira et al. take to be a polynomial of degree 1 or 2. Degree 1, , gives : the score itself. Degree 2 adds , so a -dimensional target has control variates.
  • Fitting. Mira et al. fit the coefficients by least squares, as in Part 3’s Proposition 4. These are Part 3’s Stein control variates restricted to gradient fields . Least squares minimises , the variance for independent draws, not Proposition 6’s ; Dellaportas & Kontoyiannis (2012) estimate coefficients aimed at the asymptotic variance instead.
  • Smallest instance. For , . With , the linear has , so exactly. Degree 1 removes all the variance of a Gaussian posterior mean, and degree 2 that of a second moment, since for under .
  • Without the score. Dellaportas & Kontoyiannis (2012) use from Proposition 1 in place of . That needs in closed form, as in many Gibbs samplers, and no score.

4.2 Control variates on a logistic-regression posterior

The data are synthetic: 30 points with features and labels for , seeded, of which 17 are ones. The model is logistic regression with a prior. It stands in for a small study whose posterior mean and tail probability get reported, where a few hundred extra iterations cost little but a wrong second decimal changes a conclusion. The posterior is mildly skewed, so the polynomial control variates are good but not exact.

MALA with step 0.15 samples it, accepting about 76% of proposals. The reference values come from quadrature on a grid: , and . The chart’s score is , and the evidence never appears.

The chart shows the posterior with one chain’s recent states, and that chain’s running estimates with and without control variates.

Things to try:

  1. Defaults (posterior mean of , ). The degree-2 line sits on the dashed reference almost from the first checkpoint, while the plain average wanders. Over eight sets of 20 chains of length 5,000, degree 1 cuts the mean squared error by a factor of 11.6 to 29.9 and degree 2 by 183 to 473. New chain draws another set.
  2. Second moment. Choose . Degree 1 helps less, by 2.0 to 5.5 times, because the Poisson solution for a second moment is at least quadratic. Degree 2 gives 35.6 to 96.8.
  3. Tail probability. Choose . The reductions fall to 1.5 to 3.9 for degree 1 and 2.7 to 9.5 for degree 2. The gradient of an indicator’s Poisson solution has a kink at the threshold that no low-degree polynomial follows, and by Proposition 6 the gradient error is what remains.
  4. Chain length. At the degree-2 factor for the mean is 169 to 641 across the eight sets; at it is 148 to 676. The factor does not grow with , because the residual does not depend on it.

5 Constraints

  • First order only. Equation 5 is accurate when is small. On the two-mode target, where reaches 4.2, the exact bias is 1.33 times the prediction at .
  • Expectations under . The bias coefficient and the variance are expectations under the target, which is what the sampler is for. They explain the size, sign and scaling of the errors; computing them exactly needs the one-dimensional grid of the chart.
  • One dimension in the theorem. Theorem 4 is derived in one dimension. The -dimensional form is quoted, not derived. The chart’s exact computation also needs a grid, which only works in low dimension.
  • Dimension. For , ULA’s bias is per coordinate in whatever is, but in . A statistic summed over coordinates, or the joint law, needs a step that shrinks with .
  • Polynomial control variates. They help much less for non-smooth (item 3). Degree 2 needs coefficients fitted from the chain; South et al. (2023) regularise that fit for high dimensions. Fitting the coefficients on the same chain adds a small bias.
  • Minibatch gradients. Stochastic-gradient Langevin dynamics adds gradient noise to ULA’s discretisation error. With a fixed step its kernel has a stationary law and Proposition 3 applies to it. Teh, Thiery & Vollmer (2016) analyse decreasing steps, which have no stationary law, with Poisson-equation arguments of the same kind.
  • The grid. The chart is exact up to its 241-point grid and its truncation of the line to or . A 481-point grid moves no nonzero bias by more than 0.04%.

6 Next in the series

  • Part 6: Part 2’s normal approximation bounds how far a random neural network is from its Gaussian-process limit, and Part 1’s Gaussian integration by parts explains which directions one gradient step can find.
  • Part 7: the kernel Stein discrepancy as a training regulariser for VAE latents and JEPA embeddings.

Chains. Are. Operators. Their. Mismatch. Is. Bias. Their. Solution. Is. Variance.

  • Leimkuhler, B., Matthews, C. & Stoltz, G. (2016). The computation of averages from equilibrium and nonequilibrium Langevin molecular dynamics. IMA Journal of Numerical Analysis 36(1), 13–79.
  • Mattingly, J. C., Stuart, A. M. & Tretyakov, M. V. (2010). Convergence of numerical time-averaging and stationary measures via Poisson equations. SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis 48(2), 552–577.
  • Mira, A., Solgi, R. & Imparato, D. (2013). Zero variance Markov chain Monte Carlo for Bayesian estimators. Statistics and Computing 23(5), 653–662.
  • Roberts, G. O. & Tweedie, R. L. (1996). Exponential convergence of Langevin distributions and their discrete approximations. Bernoulli 2(4), 341–363.

item.title: Stein’s Method, Part 4: Models Without Normalising Constants
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
Energy-based and other unnormalised models are hard to fit by maximum likelihood, because the likelihood gradient needs the normalising constant. The model’s score in does not, and Stein’s identity turns that score into training objectives that never compute the constant.

Energy-based models write a density as up to a constant. Diffusion models train a network to output directly. Anyone who has fitted the first kind by maximum likelihood has run a sampler inside the training loop, because the likelihood gradient contains an expectation under the model itself. The -score of the same model costs one backward pass: the normalising constant is a function of alone, so it vanishes when differentiating in . Stein’s identity is the bridge from that cheap quantity to an objective whose minimum is the right model.

Part 1 showed that the Langevin Stein operator does not see the normalising constant, and derived Stein’s unbiased risk estimate (SURE). Part 2 turned Stein identities into distances. Part 3 made the distance computable with kernels and used its steepest-descent direction, SVGD, as a sampler. This part fits models with the same tools. Part 5 applies them to MCMC samplers, Part 6 to neural networks, and Part 7 to regularising learned representations.

An AI agent (Claude) drafted the text and the interactive charts. Separate review passes checked each derivation numerically and each reference against its source.

Two ideas carry the post:

  1. Score matching is Stein’s identity under the data. The unknown data score in the Fisher divergence is removed by one integration by parts, and the Fisher divergence equals a Stein discrepancy with an -penalised critic.
  2. Stein identities are training signals. Each tool from the earlier parts becomes a loss or a gradient with no normalising constant in it: SURE trains denoisers without clean data, the Gaussian identity builds unbiased control variates for policy gradients, and SVGD’s direction trains a sampler network.

1 Notation

  • : the data distribution, with density and score ; a sample from it.
  • : the model, with . For an energy-based model, .
  • : the model’s score in .
  • : a gradient in the parameters; and without a subscript act on .
  • : the Langevin Stein operator (Parts 1 and 3).
  • : the Fisher divergence.
  • and : the SURE setting of Part 1.

2 The maximum-likelihood gradient

Differentiate the log-likelihood of one point in :

The right-hand identity differentiates under the integral, then writes and . The maximum-likelihood gradient is therefore a difference of two expectations: one under the data, and one under the model. The second needs samples from at every step, usually from an MCMC chain run inside the training loop. The derivative in has no such term:

Smallest instance: with , so . Then , which needs the model’s second moment, while the score contains no trace of .

The density in the next chart is synthetic: , a two-component mixture written without its factors. The sample is 60 seeded draws from its normalised version. It stands in for an energy-based model whose constant is never computed.

The chart shows the same split for that fixed sample. Multiplying by a constant changes its total mass and the sample’s log-likelihood. It changes nothing computed from the score.

  1. Drag from to . The left curve keeps its shape while its axis scale moves by six orders of magnitude, and the total mass goes from to .
  2. Watch the log-likelihood tile. It moves from to , a change of : the likelihood depends on through .
  3. Watch the KSD and score-matching tiles. They read and at every , to every printed digit, because the right panel’s score does not move.

3 Score matching

The Fisher divergence compares scores directly:

It contains no , but it contains the data score , which is unknown. Integration by parts removes it.

Theorem 1 — score matching (Hyvärinen 2005, Theorem 1)

Assume is positive and continuously differentiable, is continuously differentiable, and are finite, and as (Hyvärinen’s footnote 1). Assume also , which the right side needs. Then

where the constant does not depend on .

Proof.

  1. Expand the square: .
  2. The cross term is Stein’s identity under applied to the field : . Part 3’s Proposition 1 gives it: is finite because is, and is finite by Cauchy–Schwarz and the integrability of . So .
  3. Substitute into step 1 and take expectations.

The sample version replaces by the average over :

Neither nor appears. For an energy-based model, and , the Laplacian of the energy. That costs backward passes per point when computed exactly.

Smallest instance: the Gaussian model of Section 2, and . Then , minimised at , the maximum-likelihood estimate of the precision when the mean is known to be zero.

4 Fisher divergence and the penalised Stein discrepancy

Part 2 defined the Stein discrepancy as over a class of critics , and Part 3 took the class to be a kernel ball. For a class closed under the absolute value can be dropped, as here. Taking every square-integrable critic, with a penalty on its size, recovers the Fisher divergence.

Proposition 2 — the L² Stein discrepancy

Let , and let be the set of fields with that satisfy Stein’s identity under , . If , then

Proof.

  1. Subtract the zero . The divergence terms cancel: .
  2. Maximise pointwise. For each , is a concave quadratic in , maximised at with value .
  3. Take expectations under .

Grathwohl et al. (2020) state this optimal critic. The value follows by substitution. In Hyvärinen’s normalisation it is . Score matching and the -penalised Stein discrepancy therefore have the same minimiser in .

4.1 Learning the critic

Grathwohl et al. (2020) train an energy-based model against a neural critic instead of computing the Laplacian:

  • Critic step. Ascend in . By Proposition 2, the maximum over all square-integrable critics is . A neural critic reaches it only as far as its family can represent , so the inner maximum approximates it from below.
  • Model step. Only the first term depends on , so . For , this is : one backward pass through the energy’s input gradient, with no samples from the model and no .

4.2 Minimum Stein discrepancy estimators

Barp et al. (2019) take this one step further. Any Stein operator and Stein set define an estimator

with the Stein discrepancy of Part 2 and the empirical distribution of the data. They show that score matching, contrastive divergence and minimum probability flow are special cases, each with its own operator and set, and they introduce diffusion versions of KSD and of score matching. Choosing the set decides the estimator:

Stein set Discrepancy Estimator

with penalty (Proposition 2) score matching
neural critics with penalty learned approximation of Grathwohl et al. (2020)

Over the unit ball of the supremum is , by Cauchy–Schwarz. The last two rows replace the ball by a penalty. The two exact rows are and , so they have the same minimiser in as score matching. The neural-critic row shares it only when the critic family can represent . Otherwise its inner maximum falls short of by an amount that can depend on , and so can its minimiser.

5 SURE as a training loss

Part 1 derived SURE from Gaussian integration by parts: for and a weakly differentiable estimator satisfying Part 1’s integrability conditions, the risk has an unbiased estimate that does not involve . Writing it in terms of instead of the correction :

Part 1’s form follows by substituting and .

5.1 Training a denoiser without clean data

Soltanayev & Chun (2018) train a denoising network on noisy images , , each with pixels, and known, and no clean . Equation 5 makes the expected loss computable from alone. The divergence of a network is expensive, so they estimate it by a random finite difference (Ramani, Blu & Unser 2008):

One draw of per image gives their training loss:

Its gradient follows from the chain rule, with :

That is two forward passes per image, and a backward pass through each.

  • What the first term does. On its own it would train to reproduce the noisy input, the identity map.
  • What the divergence term does. It penalises sensitivity to the input in proportion to , which is what keeps from copying the noise.
  • Settings in the paper. is redrawn every epoch. is small and fixed: for their MNIST denoiser and for DnCNN.

5.2 Choosing a regularisation strength

The same identity chooses a single parameter in closed form. For soft thresholding, , the correction is when and otherwise.

  1. .

  2. when and when . The estimator is Lipschitz, so the kinks at do not matter. Hence almost surely.

  3. Substituting into Part 1’s :

This is the SURE criterion of Donoho & Johnstone (1995), stated there for . Their SureShrink applies it to each wavelet level, and falls back to the threshold on levels that look sparse. Minimising it over uses only . For ridge shrinkage, , the same steps give

The signal in the chart is synthetic: 256 coordinates, 25 of them nonzero with magnitudes drawn between 2 and 6, observed once in Gaussian noise of known . It stands in for the wavelet coefficients of an image: a few large values among many near-zero ones. A wrong either keeps the noise (too small) or erases the signal (too large).

The chart shows SURE() and the true loss against for one noisy draw, with stat tiles for the each one picks. The true loss needs the clean signal and is plotted only for comparison; in practice only SURE is available.

Things to try:

  1. At the defaults (soft threshold, ), SURE picks with a true loss of , while the oracle’s gives . The raw observation’s loss is .
  2. Press New noise draw several times. SURE’s curve is noisier than the loss curve, and its minimiser moves more. Over eight draws at , SURE’s ranges over and the oracle’s over . The loss at SURE’s is 0.3% to 22% above the oracle’s.
  3. Switch to ridge shrinkage. Over eight draws at , SURE’s stays within 0.10 of the oracle’s (up to 0.58 for soft thresholding), and the loss there is at most 0.6% above the oracle’s. On the first draw (reload the page to return to it), the best ridge loss is , against for soft thresholding. Shrinking every coordinate by the same factor cannot keep large values while zeroing small ones.
  4. Move between 0.25 and 2. SURE’s stays near the oracle’s at small and drifts further at large . On the first draw, SURE’s choice costs at most 2.3% more loss than the oracle’s up to , even where the two values differ by about 0.3, because the loss curve is flat near its minimum. At it costs 9% more. Over eight draws at each on the slider, the loss at SURE’s is at most 26% above the oracle’s (the worst case is at ). Equation 7 is unbiased for the risk at every , and summing over 256 coordinates keeps its noise small next to the risk.

6 Stein control variates for policy gradients

The policy-gradient theorem writes the gradient of expected return as . That is a score-function estimator, with high variance. Subtracting a baseline keeps it unbiased because . A baseline that also depends on the action, , can track much more closely, but it biases the gradient unless the term it adds is corrected for. Liu et al. (2018) supply the correction from Stein’s identity. In this section is a state, not a score, and is the map that turns noise into an action (Liu et al. write ).

Proposition 3 — Stein’s identity for reparameterisable policies (Liu et al. 2018, Theorem 3.1)

Let the action be with independent of , and let be differentiable. Under conditions that allow differentiation under the integral,

Proof. Compute two ways.

  1. Score function. , the left side of Equation 8.
  2. Reparameterisation. , the right side.

Both compute the same derivative.

For a Gaussian policy with mean and fixed covariance , , and Equation 8 with respect to the mean parameters reduces to . That is Part 1’s Gaussian integration by parts in the action.

Adding and subtracting gives the Stein control-variate gradient, unbiased for every (Liu et al. 2018, eq. 8):

  • The estimator. The sample version averages the bracket over observed , with an estimate in place of .
  • Fitting . Liu et al. parametrise . They fit either by regressing on observed returns, or by minimising the squared norm of the bracket in Equation 9, a direct proxy for the estimator’s variance. That objective mixes derivatives in and , which the paper finds hard to compute efficiently with automatic differentiation. For Gaussian policies it minimises instead, the variances of the gradient estimates for the policy’s mean and covariance.
  • Keeping it unbiased. Fitting on the same data the gradient uses biases the estimate. Liu et al. note that fitting on the previous iteration’s data removes the bias. Their experiments use the current data, and a check with previous-iteration data did not improve results.
  • Smallest instance. , with no action dependence, gives , and Equation 9 reduces to the ordinary baseline.

7 Amortised SVGD

SVGD (Part 3) moves a fixed set of particles. A sampler network , , needs a rule for moving its weights instead. Wang & Liu (2016) pull SVGD’s direction back through the network.

  1. Draw and set .

  2. Compute the SVGD direction on this batch:

  3. Ask the network to output instead. One gradient step on at the current , with unit step length, gives their update:

The gradient of that squared error at the current is , so the step is backpropagation of SVGD’s direction through the generator.

  • Smallest instance. A location family, , has . The repulsion terms cancel in the sum over , because for a translation-invariant kernel. The update reduces to , which moves the network’s location toward high target density.
  • A direct KSD penalty. The alternative minimises itself (Part 3). Its gradient in is , and contains , so it needs , the Hessian of . Amortised SVGD needs only . Both are free of .
  • In this blog. Nuisance Leakage in JEPA Embeddings uses a KSD penalty toward on an encoder’s embeddings. That target has , which makes the Hessian term free.

8 Constraints

  • Kernel and bandwidth. KSD-based objectives inherit Part 3’s kernel choice: light-tailed kernels can certify a non-converging sample in , and a bad bandwidth stalls or over-smooths SVGD.
  • Dimension. Kernel distances between points concentrate as grows, which should be expected to weaken KSD tests and SVGD’s repulsion. Anastasiou et al. (2023) list sliced Stein discrepancies as one way to cut the cost of Stein discrepancies in high dimensions.
  • Low-density regions. weights score errors by . Where the data are rare, a wrong score costs almost nothing, so a fitted score is least reliable where a sampler started from noise begins.
  • Isolated components. Fisher divergence, KSD and SVGD cannot see the mixing weights of well-separated components (Wenliang & Kanagawa 2020). Part 3’s chart reproduces this: a sample sitting entirely on the lighter mode has a lower KSD than an exact sample.
  • Second derivatives. Score matching needs , which is backward passes. A learned critic replaces it with , which avoids differentiating the energy twice but is still passes when computed exactly. A random-projection estimate, as in Equation 6, cuts either trace to one pass per probe at the cost of variance.
  • SURE’s assumptions. SURE needs Gaussian noise with known and a weakly differentiable estimator. With a Monte Carlo divergence, trades the finite-difference bias against round-off.

9 Next in the series

  • Part 5: the Langevin operator applied to gradients is the generator of the Langevin diffusion. Its Stein equation is the Poisson equation of MCMC, whose solution sets the bias of unadjusted Langevin and the variance of exact samplers.
  • Part 6: Stein’s lemma bounds how far a random network is from a Gaussian process and explains which directions one gradient step can learn; its closing map places score matching, SURE and SVGD in machine learning.
  • Part 7: the kernel Stein discrepancy of a batch of codes as a regulariser in a VAE and a JEPA, compared with KL, MMD, VICReg and SIGReg.

10 Further reading

  • Anastasiou et al. (2023) review Stein’s method in computational statistics: discrepancies, samplers, goodness-of-fit tests and estimators.
  • Ley, Reinert & Swan (2017) survey Stein operators for univariate distributions, beyond the Langevin form used in this series.
  • Barp et al. (2019) give the general minimum Stein discrepancy framework, with consistency, asymptotic normality and robustness results.
  • Part 1, Part 2 and Part 3 of this series derive every identity Part 4 uses.

Constants. Cancel. Scores. Remain. Stein. Turns. Scores. Into. Losses.

11 References

  • Barp, A., Briol, F.-X., Duncan, A., Girolami, M. & Mackey, L. (2019). Minimum Stein discrepancy estimators. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32.
  • Donoho, D. L. & Johnstone, I. M. (1995). Adapting to unknown smoothness via wavelet shrinkage. Journal of the American Statistical Association 90(432), 1200–1224.

  • Hyvärinen, A. (2005). Estimation of non-normalized statistical models by score matching. Journal of Machine Learning Research 6, 695–709.

  • Liu, H., Feng, Y., Mao, Y., Zhou, D., Peng, J. & Liu, Q. (2018). Action-dependent control variates for policy optimization via Stein identity. International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2018).

item.title: Stein’s Method, Part 3: Kernel Stein Discrepancy and SVGD
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
The kernel Stein discrepancy (KSD) measures how far a sample is from a target density using only the target’s score, in closed form. Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) moves a set of particles along the direction in which the same kernel says KL divergence falls fastest.

MCMC output is usually checked with trace plots, and effective sample size. Those compare chains with one another, not with the target. A sampler with a bias, such as unadjusted Langevin with a large step or stochastic-gradient Langevin with minibatch noise, can mix well and settle on the wrong distribution, and every between-chain check still passes. Catching that needs a comparison of the sample with the target itself. The target is usually known only up to its normalising constant, so the comparison has to go through the score. Part 2’s Stein discrepancy does this, but it is a supremum over a class of functions. Taking that class to be a ball in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space turns the supremum into a double sum.

Part 1 built the Langevin Stein operator and showed that it does not see the normalising constant. Part 2 turned Stein identities into distances. Part 4 uses the same discrepancy to fit models. Part 5 predicts the bias and variance of MCMC samplers instead of measuring them after the run. Part 6 turns to neural networks, and Part 7 adds this part’s discrepancy to training losses.

An AI agent (Claude) drafted the text and the interactive chart. Separate review passes checked each derivation numerically and each reference against its source.

Three ideas carry the post:

  1. Kernel Stein discrepancy. With ranging over the unit ball of a kernel’s Hilbert space, has a closed form: the square root of for an explicit Stein kernel .
  2. SVGD. The function that attains that supremum is the direction of steepest descent of among small kernel-smooth moves of the sample. Moving particles along it is a sampler.
  3. Stein control variates. has mean zero under for every in the Stein class, so it can be subtracted from an integrand to reduce Monte Carlo variance.

1 Notation

  • : the target density on ; an unnormalised version; its score.
  • : the law of the sample; the sample.
  • for a vector field (Part 1).
  • : a positive definite kernel; its reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), in which .
  • : vector fields with each , and .
  • Two kernels:
    • RBF, , with bandwidth .
    • Inverse multiquadric (IMQ), with and . The default is , .

2 Stein’s identity in dimensions

Part 1 proved the one-dimensional identity and stated this one. The KSD closed form, the SVGD direction and the control variates all rest on it.

Proposition 1 — the Langevin identity in

Let be positive and continuously differentiable on , and let be a continuously differentiable vector field with and . Then

Proof.

  1. , by the product rule.
  2. On the ball of radius , the divergence theorem gives , where is the outward normal.
  3. Write . In polar coordinates, , so cannot stay bounded away from zero. There is a sequence with , and the boundary flux in step 2 is at most in absolute value.
  4. Along , the left side of step 2 tends to by dominated convergence, and the right side tends to 0.

The integrability of under plays the role of Part 1’s condition that vanishes at an infinite end.

3 Kernel Stein discrepancy

Part 2 defined the Stein discrepancy and left the supremum as an optimisation. A Hilbert-space ball makes it a projection. The closed form uses two RKHS facts:

  • Reproducing property. .
  • Derivative reproducing property. If has continuous mixed partial derivatives , then . Here is the derivative in the first argument, and it is itself in .
Definition — kernel Stein discrepancy

The ball is symmetric, so the supremum of the expectation equals the supremum of its absolute value.

Theorem 2 — closed form (Liu, Lee & Jordan 2016; Chwialkowski, Strathmann & Gretton 2016)

Let have continuous mixed partial derivatives, and define the Stein kernel

If , then

with and independent.

The formula is from the two papers in the title. The integrability condition is the one in Gorham & Mackey (2017, Proposition 2); Chwialkowski et al. assume the stronger .

Proof.

  1. The operator as an inner product. For , the two reproducing properties give

  2. Take expectations inside. Expanding with the reproducing properties gives the -th term of . So . Each is therefore Bochner integrable (integrable as a random element of ), lies in , and .

  3. The supremum is a norm. with . By Cauchy–Schwarz its supremum over the unit ball is , attained at .

  4. Expand the norm. . Expanding each inner product with the reproducing properties gives the four terms of Equation 2, coordinate by coordinate.

Three consequences:

  • No normalising constant. depends on only through , which is the same for and (Part 1).
  • No samples from . Only the sample from enters.
  • Zero at the target. For fixed , is applied to the field . When and its first and mixed second derivatives are bounded, as for the RBF and IMQ kernels, and , that field meets the conditions of Proposition 1. Then Equation 1 gives , and .

Smallest instance. Take , (so ) and the RBF kernel. With , , and . The four terms collapse to

3.1 Estimators

Replacing by the sample gives two estimators of , each to compute:

  • V-statistic, . It is the squared KSD of the empirical measure itself, so it is never negative. It is biased upward: its mean is .
  • U-statistic, . It is unbiased for and can be negative.

Goodness-of-fit tests use these as test statistics. When the U-statistic is degenerate, so its limit law is not normal, and the tests calibrate with a bootstrap. Liu, Lee & Jordan (2016) use the U-statistic. Chwialkowski, Strathmann & Gretton (2016) use the V-statistic with a wild bootstrap, which reweights the terms with random signs drawn along the chain and so also handles correlated MCMC samples.

The V-statistic does not vanish on an exact sample at finite . For 100 exact draws from the banana target of Section 5, the IMQ KSD ranges from 0.30 to 0.43 over five seeds. That is the noise floor any finite i.i.d. sample sits on.

3.2 Kernel choice

Gorham & Mackey (2017) separate kernels that make KSD a reliable convergence check from kernels that do not:

  • Light tails fail in . For the standard normal target in , KSD with the Gaussian, Matérn or compactly supported Wendland kernel can go to zero along a sequence of samples that does not converge to the target (their Theorem 6). The kernel’s features decay too fast to penalise mass drifting away.
  • IMQ succeeds. With the IMQ kernel (, ), implies weak convergence for every target that is distantly dissipative with a Lipschitz score (their Theorem 8). Distantly dissipative means the score points back toward the bulk at long range, with . Their examples include finite Gaussian mixtures with a common covariance, and Bayesian linear, logistic and Huber regression posteriors with Gaussian priors. Of the chart’s three targets only the mixture is in this class: the banana’s score grows like and is not distantly dissipative along the ridge, and the donut’s score is not Lipschitz at the origin.
  • One dimension is safe. In , for targets in the same distantly dissipative class, any kernel with twice continuously differentiable and a non-vanishing generalised Fourier transform works, Gaussian included (their Theorem 5). Neither Theorem 5 nor Theorem 6 covers , so for Gaussian and Matérn kernels in two dimensions the paper says nothing either way.

The chart in Section 5 uses the IMQ kernel with and , the default of Gorham & Mackey (2017). Its targets are two-dimensional, so it cannot show the failure.

4 Stein variational gradient descent

KSD measures a distance, and its maximiser is a direction: the direction in which the sample most violates Stein’s identity. Moving the sample along that direction reduces the KL divergence fastest.

Theorem 3 — steepest descent of KL (Liu & Wang 2016, Theorem 3.1 and Lemma 3.2)

Let and be smooth positive densities. For a smooth field and small , let , and let be the law of when . Under regularity conditions that allow differentiation under the integral,

Over with , the fastest decrease is , attained at , where

Proof.

  1. Move the map onto . KL divergence is unchanged when the same invertible map is applied to both arguments. So , and has density .
  2. Write it out. . For small the determinant is positive.
  3. Differentiate at . and . Together these give Equation 4.
  4. Optimise over the ball. By step 3 of Theorem 2’s proof, , which is maximised over the unit ball at with value . By the reproducing property, , which is Equation 5.

Liu & Wang (2016) state the same result over the ball of radius , where the optimal direction is itself and the derivative is .

4.1 The particle update

Replace by the current particles and step along (Liu & Wang 2016, Algorithm 1):

  • Driving force. A kernel-weighted average of the scores at nearby particles pulls toward high density, smoothed over the bandwidth.
  • Repulsion. For the RBF kernel, . It points from toward , so it pushes particles apart. Without it, every particle would climb to a mode.
  • One particle. With , for a translation-invariant kernel, and Equation 6 becomes gradient ascent on . One SVGD particle finds a mode.
  • Bandwidth. Liu & Wang (2016) write the RBF kernel as and set , where is the median pairwise distance between particles, so that . In this post’s convention, that is .
  • Step size. Liu & Wang use AdaGrad, which scales each coordinate’s step by its past gradients. The chart uses a fixed , so that the comparison with Langevin uses one step size for both.

4.2 Gradient flow

As and then , with time measured as times the number of steps, the limiting particle density follows the continuity equation (Liu 2017). Along it the KL divergence falls at a rate set by the KSD (Liu 2017, Theorem 3.4):

  • The second equality integrates by parts once, with boundary terms assumed to vanish.
  • The third applies Equation 1 under : .
  • The fourth is step 4 of Theorem 3, with .

Langevin dynamics obeys the same identity with the Fisher divergence in place of (Liu 2017, §3.5). Part 4 returns to that divergence.

5 SVGD and Langevin on three targets

The targets are synthetic two-dimensional densities, each written as an unnormalised log-density and its score. Each stands in for a posterior shape that breaks simpler samplers:

  • Banana: and . A curved ridge, like the posterior of a model that identifies only a product or a square of its parameters.
  • Mixture: with separation . Two explanations of the data with unequal weight.
  • Donut: . Mass on a ring, like a posterior constrained near a sphere.

A wrong answer here means reporting posterior means and intervals from a sample that misses part of the target, or weights it wrongly.

The comparison holds the budget fixed. SVGD moves particles; unadjusted Langevin (ULA) runs independent chains, with . Both start from the same points and use the same step size and number of iterations, so both make score evaluations per iteration. SVGD also pays kernel evaluations per iteration, which the count leaves out.

The chart shows both point sets over the target’s contours, and their KSD against score evaluations.

Things to try:

  1. Defaults (banana, , , median-heuristic bandwidth). Press Play. Langevin is ahead at first: after 50 iterations its KSD is lower on all five seeds checked (0.27 to 0.40, against 0.42 to 0.61 for SVGD). Langevin’s trace is noisy, so the two curves cross back and forth for a while: SVGD first drops below it between iterations 31 and 61, and stays below from somewhere between iteration 77 and 119, depending on the seed. After 500 iterations it reaches 0.060 to 0.067, against 0.22 to 0.38 for Langevin, which sits near the 0.30 to 0.43 floor of 100 exact draws.
  2. Step size. Press Reset, set to 0.1 and press Play. Langevin diverges on the banana on every seed checked, because its step is too large for the score’s steep walls. From this start SVGD stays finite up to 0.2 on all 20 seeds checked, because the kernel average damps each particle’s step. Its stability has limits. Started at with , SVGD diverges on 5 of 10 seeds, and the widget then marks it as diverged too.
  3. Bandwidth. Press Reset, untick the median heuristic, set and press Play. The kernel weight between distinct particles is now close to zero, so the driving force shrinks to about : each particle runs its own gradient ascent with step , and only near neighbours still repel. The particles slide onto the ridge and bunch closer to it than the target does, and KSD is still 0.72 to 0.97 after 500 iterations. Press Reset again and set : the kernel averages scores over too wide an area, and KSD ends at 0.16 to 0.24. With (after another Reset) it ends at 0.051 to 0.067, about where the median heuristic lands (0.055 to 0.070, with settling near 0.57). These ranges cover 20 seeds, so they hold however many times Reset has been pressed.
  4. Missing mode. Choose the mixture, set the separation to 8 and the initial centre to 4, so every particle starts on the lighter mode. After 1,000 iterations SVGD has kept all of them there: the share with is 1.00, against a target of 0.30. Across 20 seeds KSD reads 0.042 to 0.051, lower than for 100 exact draws from the mixture (0.16 to 0.25). The heavy mode is too far away for the kernel or the score to see.
  5. Same mixture, centred start. Set . The particles split between the modes, but after 1,000 iterations 0.33 to 0.54 of them sit on the lighter one across 20 seeds, with a median of 0.43. Exact draws would put 0.30 there, give or take 0.05.

Item 4 is a blindness of score-based methods in general: far from a component, the score carries almost no information about that component’s weight (Wenliang & Kanagawa 2020). A low KSD certifies the sample against the score, and the score does not know about modes it has not visited.

6 Using KSD on MCMC output

The same discrepancy that drives SVGD can audit any sampler’s output.

6.1 A sample-quality check

Compute the KSD of a sampler’s output against . Unlike between-chain diagnostics, it compares the sample with the target. It can therefore rank step sizes or approximate samplers by how close their output is to , not only by how well they mix. Gorham & Mackey (2015) introduced Stein discrepancies for this purpose. Liu, Lee & Jordan (2016) and Chwialkowski et al. (2016) gave the kernel closed form, and Gorham & Mackey (2017) showed which kernels make it a reliable convergence check.

6.2 Stein thinning

MCMC output is usually thinned by keeping every tenth or hundredth point after a burn-in. Stein thinning (Riabiz et al. 2022) instead picks points greedily to make the selected set’s KSD small:

The rule is greedy minimisation of the V-statistic. Adding a point to a selected set of size raises the double sum , which is of the enlarged set, by , half of which is Equation 7.

  • Points are selected with replacement, so an index can repeat.
  • The cost is at most for selected points.
  • Riabiz et al. use an IMQ base kernel with a preconditioner.

6.3 Stein points

Stein points (Chen et al. 2018) use the same greedy objective, minimised over all of instead of over a chain’s output, starting from a global maximum of . That start agrees with the objective: at the first step it is alone, and for the IMQ kernel , which every stationary point of minimises.

7 Stein control variates

Estimating by a sample average has variance . Subtracting a function with known mean zero leaves the mean unchanged and can cut the variance. Stein’s identity produces such functions from any in the Stein class, using only the score.

Proposition 4 — Stein control variates

Let satisfy the conditions of Proposition 1, and let . Assume and have finite variance under , and that is positive definite. Then, for every :

  1. .
  2. is minimised at , where .
  3. The minimum is , where is the squared multiple correlation between and .

Proof.

  1. by Equation 1.
  2. , a convex quadratic in . Its gradient vanishes at .
  3. Substituting, .

Smallest instance. Take and , which has .

  • gives .
  • gives .
  • With alone, and , so the variance falls from 3 to 2 ().
  • With both, : zero variance, and the estimate is exact.

Polynomial remove polynomial completely under a Gaussian target.

In practice is estimated from the same sample, which adds a small bias unless the sample is split.

Control functionals (Oates, Girolami & Chopin 2017) let range over instead of a finite family. Then ranges over an RKHS whose kernel is the Stein kernel of Equation 2. Adding constants gives the kernel .

  1. Fit. Fit by kernel ridge regression with . The fit is with , where and .

  2. Integrate the fit. (Section 3), so , and the fitted function integrates to .

  3. Simplify. With and the Sherman–Morrison formula,

This is a weighted sum of the , with weights that do not depend on and sum to just under one for small . Oates et al. define the estimator with sample splitting, where one part of the sample fits and the other averages, and prove a mean squared error of under their conditions. They recommend the unsplit form Equation 8 for its lower variance.

8 Unnormalised posteriors

For a Bayesian posterior , with prior and likelihood , the score is

The evidence never appears. KSD (Equation 2), the SVGD direction (Equation 5), Stein thinning (Equation 7) and control functionals (Equation 8) take only from the target.

Smallest instance: logistic regression with a prior, features and labels . The score is , with the logistic function. It costs one pass over the data, the same as a gradient step.

9 Constraints

  • Mode blindness. KSD and SVGD see only the score along the sample. A component far from every particle contributes nothing, so a sample that misses it can have a lower KSD than an exact sample (item 4).
  • Kernel choice. In , light-tailed kernels can certify a non-converging sample. Use IMQ with for convergence checks.
  • Dimension. Each kernel evaluation compares -dimensional vectors, and kernel distances concentrate as grows, so KSD tests and SVGD’s repulsion should be expected to weaken in high dimensions. Neither is checked here beyond .
  • Cost. KSD, SVGD and Stein thinning are per evaluation or step. Control functionals solve an linear system.
  • Bandwidth. Too small a bandwidth turns SVGD into slow independent gradient ascent, and too large a bandwidth over-smooths it (item 3). The median heuristic is a rule of thumb, not a guarantee.
  • Finite-sample floor. The V-statistic KSD of an exact i.i.d. sample is positive: 0.30 to 0.43 for 100 banana draws. Interacting particles can go below it, and so can a sample that misses a mode (item 4), so a value below the floor does not by itself certify a sample.

10 Next in the series

  • Part 4 turns the same machinery on model fitting. With a ball in instead of an RKHS, the Stein discrepancy becomes the square root of the Fisher divergence of score matching; with an penalty in place of the ball, it becomes the Fisher divergence itself, up to a constant. Stein identities then supply training losses for denoisers, control variates for policy gradients, and a generator update that pulls SVGD’s direction back to network weights.
  • Part 5 returns to MCMC. The Langevin operator applied to gradients is the generator of the Langevin diffusion; its Stein equation gives unadjusted Langevin’s bias to first order in the step, the asymptotic variance of exact samplers, and Section 7’s control variates restricted to gradient fields.
  • Part 6 applies Stein’s lemma to neural networks and maps where KSD and SVGD are used in machine learning.
  • Part 7 uses KSD to N(0, I) as a training regulariser: the length of the SVGD step a batch of codes would take. In 64 dimensions a wide kernel sees little more than the first two moments.
  • Nuisance Leakage in JEPA Embeddings uses KSD to with an IMQ kernel as an anti-collapse regulariser for a self-supervised encoder.

Kernels. Close. The. Supremum. Particles. Follow. It. Modes. Hide.

item.title: Stein’s Method, Part 2: Normal Approximation
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
Stein’s method bounds the distance between a random variable’s law and the normal by solving one differential equation per test function. For a normalised sum of independent terms it gives a Wasserstein distance of order , with explicit constants.

Normal approximations are usually justified by the central limit theorem and a rule of thumb such as . The theorem is a limit statement: it says the error goes to zero, not how large it is at the in hand. Thirty summands are plenty for a uniform, whose standardised sum is then from the normal in Wasserstein distance. They are nowhere near enough for a Bernoulli with , where the distance at is . Berry–Esseen-type theorems give a rate. Stein’s method proves one in a page, with constants that can be computed, and the same template extends to dependent terms and to other limit laws.

Part 1 showed that over a rich class of characterises the standard normal, and that its proof writes as an expectation of that form. This part makes that equality quantitative. Part 3 makes the resulting discrepancy computable from samples, Part 4 uses it to fit models, Part 5 runs the generator approach on MCMC samplers, Part 6 applies Theorem 4 and its refinements to random neural networks, and Part 7 trains with the discrepancy as a regulariser.

An AI agent (Claude) drafted the text and the interactive chart. Separate review passes checked each derivation numerically and each reference against its source.

Three ideas carry the post:

  1. The Stein equation. For a test function , the solution of converts the error into , an expectation under alone.
  2. Bounds on the solution. For Lipschitz , and its first two derivatives are bounded by constant multiples of . A bound on that holds uniformly over that small class of therefore bounds the Wasserstein distance.
  3. Leave one out. For a sum of independent terms, removing one term at a time and expanding to second order gives that uniform bound. The third and fourth moments of the terms supply the constants.

2 Integral probability metrics

A distance between laws can be defined by how differently they integrate a set of test functions.

5 Sums of independent terms

Lemma 3 places every with in the class

Theorem 4 — Wasserstein bound for sums (Ross 2011, Theorem 3.2)

Let be independent with , and , and let . Then

Proof. Fix .

5.1 The bound against exact distances

The summands are synthetic. Four laws, each standardised to mean 0 and variance 1, cover the cases the theorem treats differently. Each stands in for a quantity averaged over independent units:

  1. Choose the exponential and move from 1 to 200. The histogram’s right skew shrinks. The exact falls from 0.314 to 0.0228, and the bound from 4.81 to 0.340.

6 Other couplings and operators

Leave-one-out needs independence. The same Stein equation and the same bounds on support other ways of controlling . All four need posts of their own, so here they get one line each.

  • Exchangeable pairs (Stein 1986): build with exchangeable and , then expand . This handles statistics of a whole dependent system, such as the anti-voter model (Ross 2011, §3.3.1); local dependence is usually handled with dependency neighbourhoods instead (Ross 2011, §3.2).
  • Zero-bias couplings (Goldstein & Reinert 1997; Goldstein 2010): build with . Then , which is at most . By Part 1, the normal is the only law with .
  • Chen–Stein Poisson approximation (Chen 1975): the Poisson() law has its own operator, , and the same template bounds the distance from a count of rare, weakly dependent events to the Poisson.
  • The generator approach (Barbour 1988, 1990): choose a Markov process whose stationary law is the target. Its generator is a Stein operator. For the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, Section 4 shows its semigroup solving the Stein equation.

7 The Stein discrepancy

Replace by a density on and the Gaussian operator by the Langevin operator of Part 1. Replace by a sample from a law . The supremum in Corollary 2 becomes the Stein discrepancy (Gorham & Mackey 2015), with called the Stein set:

  • What it needs. Samples from , to estimate , and the score . It does not need ’s normalising constant, since (Part 1). It does not need samples from .
  • Why it measures distance. If contains a solution of for every , the argument of Corollary 2 gives . Bounding those solutions for a non-Gaussian plays the role of Lemma 3, and is harder.
  • Why it is hard to compute. The supremum is an optimisation over functions. Gorham & Mackey (2015) solve it as a linear program over a graph built on the sample points.

Smallest instance: in one dimension and . By Equation 3, exactly.

8 Constraints

  • Moments. Theorem 4 needs ; the zero-bias route needs third moments. Heavier tails fall outside both.
  • Independence. Step 1 of the proof uses , which fails under dependence. Exchangeable pairs and couplings (Section 6) are the replacements.
  • Wasserstein, not Kolmogorov. Converting through halves the rate to . A direct Kolmogorov bound needs the non-smooth .
  • Constants. The bound exceeds the exact distance by 3.6 to 15.5 times at for the Bernoulli, exponential and mixture laws in the chart, and by 443 times for the uniform, whose true rate is .

9 Next in the series

  • Part 3: with the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space of vector fields, Equation 5 becomes a double expectation of a kernel. It is computed from samples in time, and its steepest-descent direction moves particles toward .
  • Part 4: with a ball in , the same discrepancy becomes the Fisher divergence that score matching minimises, up to a square or a constant.
  • Part 5: the generator approach of Section 6, run for the Langevin diffusion. Its Stein equation is the Poisson equation, whose solution gives the bias of unadjusted Langevin and the variance of MCMC averages.
  • Part 6: Theorem 4 applies to a random network’s output, a sum over hidden units. Conditioning on the hidden layer improves its to .
  • Part 7: the Stein discrepancy of a batch of codes as a training loss for a VAE and a JEPA.

Solve. Stein’s. Equation. Bound. Solutions. Leave. One. Out. Rates. Follow.

item.title: Stein’s Method, Part 1: Stein’s Lemma
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
Stein’s lemma characterises the standard normal by one expectation identity that must hold for every test function in a class, instead of by a list of moments. Rewritten for any smooth density, the identity needs only the derivative of the log-density, so it still works when the density’s normalising constant is unknown.

Checking whether data look normal usually means a histogram, a QQ plot, or the first few moments. Moments are a weak check. After standardising, the uniform, the Laplace and the normal share their mean and variance, and no finite list of matched moments pins a law down. Stein’s lemma replaces the list with one identity required of a whole class of test functions. Each contributes one equation, and the class as a whole leaves only the normal standing. The general-density version is what makes the idea useful beyond normality: it tests a sample against a density whose integral nobody can compute.

This is the first of seven parts. Part 2 turns the identity into a bound on the distance between a sum and the normal. Part 3 makes that distance computable from samples and uses it to move particles toward a target. Part 4 fits models whose normalising constant is unknown. Part 5 gives the bias and variance of MCMC samplers. Part 6 applies the identity to neural networks. Part 7 uses the discrepancy built from it as a training regulariser.

An AI agent (Claude) drafted the text and the interactive chart. Separate review passes checked each derivation numerically and each reference against its source.

Three ideas carry the post:

  1. Stein’s identity. holds for every suitable when , and for no other law.
  2. The Langevin Stein operator. The same construction for a density uses only through its score , so an unknown normalising constant drops out.
  3. Stein’s unbiased risk estimate (SURE). For a Gaussian observation, the identity turns an estimator’s expected squared error, which depends on the unknown mean, into a quantity computed from the data.

1 Notation

  • : a standard normal variable. is its density and its distribution function.
  • : a random variable being compared with .
  • : a density, positive on an interval with .
  • : an unnormalised version of , with normalising constant . The calligraphic keeps free for the normal variable.
  • : the score function of , the derivative of the log-density in . It is not a scoring rule.
  • : the Stein operator of (Section 5).
  • for a function ; is the Euclidean norm for a vector .
  • A function is absolutely continuous if for all . Every continuously differentiable is, and so is a continuous with finitely many kinks.

2 Stein’s identity for the standard normal

The normal density satisfies , and it is the only density that does. Integrating by parts moves the derivative onto , and that equation turns the result into an expectation of :

The content of the lemma is the conditions under which both integrals exist and the boundary term is zero.

Lemma 1 — Stein’s identity (Ross 2011, Lemma 2.1)

7 Constraints

  • Boundary terms. The identity needs the boundary term to vanish. On the whole line, is enough. A density that stays positive at an end of a bounded support, as for the uniform or a truncated normal, breaks it unless takes the same value at both ends, for instance because vanishes there. The uniform with gives 3, not 0.
  • Integrability. binds for heavy tails. Under Student-, needs for the Langevin operator and for the Gaussian one, and Monte Carlo error bars need and respectively.
  • One test function is one equation. A characterisation needs a class rich enough to see the distribution function; Lemma 2’s class is one, because it contains the indicator solutions . With alone, every standardised law passes.

8 Next in the series

  • Part 2: Lemma 2’s proof solved the Stein equation for one indicator. Solving it for every test function in a class turns a small into a bound on a distance between and , with explicit constants, and gives the central limit theorem with a rate.
  • Part 3: the -dimensional Langevin operator, with ranging over a kernel space, gives a discrepancy that is computed from a sample and the score, with no normalising constant.

  • Part 7: the identity, tested on a batch of codes over a class of functions, becomes a training loss. Over affine functions it is the moment penalty of self-supervised learning.

One. Identity. Pins. Normals. Scores. Ignore. Constants. Boundaries. Decide.

  • Stein’s Method, Part 4: Models Without Normalising Constants — score matching and Stein-based training losses.
